title: Advanced Predicaments
about:
In this course, Fred Hatt teaches two advanced predicament ties with his model Briki. In both classes, he shares detailed explanations about balance, body mechanics and build-up (of ties and endorphins) for both riggers and rope bottoms. The ties taught in this course both require a suspension point. 


Predicaments are Fred's favourite form of rope play. Endurance, impossible choices, and playing with his bottom’s headspace are the key ingredients in the equation. These ties can be difficult to achieve without good knowledge of the body and in this form of play rigger and model are working ‘against’ each other rather that with each other, so it becomes important to recognise ways in which the model can ‘cheat’ while always paying extreme attention to detail and body cues to keep the bottom safe. 


In the first class, Fred teaches a simple form of his signature 'Pyramid Tie'. This tie is a perfect entry point to Predicament Play, using only simple knots while conveying clearly the concept of threat vs effort in a tie. 


In the second class, Fred teaches the 'Misery Tie' a more advanced and challenging predicament form. At the end of the class, Fred and Briki share some feedback and extra information about their experience playing with this tie. 


Expect hair ties, crotch ropes and burning muscles... This course is not for the faint of heart!

Using the principles taught in this series makes for a more experimental and flowing approach to rope than some more structured types of tying, making it ideal for playful sessions.

title: Reverse Prayer Tie
about:
In this shibari class, Ropunawa teaches his take on the Reverse Prayer Tie with his model Freya.


Ropunawa’s latest class is a structural-but-fun challenge for both rigger and model alike. With hands tied in a ‘prayer’ position behind the back, the Reverse Prayer Tie is a visually striking harness that relies as much on the shoulder flexibility of the person being tied as it relies on the skill of the person doing the tying. An essential check to do before beginning is to see if the model’s hands comfortably fit into the space between their shoulder – with that confirmed, you can go ahead and get started with this rewarding tie.


This tie is suitable for all students from intermediate level up, however, it is not suitable for every model. Only attempt to do it if their flexibility allows for it.

title: M-Shape Suspension
about:
In this video, Gestalta teaches a simple 'M-shape' suspension with their model Aleks.

This tie can be kept close to the ground as a partial suspension or lifted into a full suspension either by using a pulley or incrementally, as demonstrated in the class. This class is ideal for intermediate level students wanting to play with suspension in a safe and relaxing way, giving the opportunity to experiment with variations within the original structure.

For this tie, Gestalta is using their Spellbound TK but feel free to replace it with any chest harness of your choice. Recommended harnesses for safer suspensions include the Butterfly, Xana, Misungui and Fisherman harnesses.

For expert users who wish to spice things up and feel confident using more demanding upper-body structures, you can replace the TK with harnesses like a Strappado, Tengu or Teppo, for example. If you choose to increase the difficulty by using more challenging chest harnesses, we highly recommend first experimenting with a partial suspension before attempting to fully suspend.

title: Yoko Tsuri Study
about:
In this course, Gestalta demonstrates and explains different variations of Yoko-tsuri (side suspension) with their model Aleks.

This class is ideal if you are fairly new to suspension and want to practice a position that is not too challenging for the model and doesn't involve advanced uplines management.


In the first part, they demonstrate a side suspension without hip support, with a few tips on how to get into the position smoothly. They show a few variations and explains the pros and cons of this simple execution of the tie.


In the second part, they demonstrate a side suspension with hip support by using a more supportive tie on the leg as well as adding either a wrap around the hips or a gun slinger harness.


In both classes, they show how the same position can look and feel different by changing the levels of the upper-body in relation to the lower-body and playing around with variations with the remaining leg.


Note that Gestalta is using a TK in the classes, but you can replace it with a hands-free harness to reduce the risk of nerve damage and stress in the shoulders.

title: Masterclass: Nerve Compression Management (FREE)
about:
In this voice-over lecture, Ms. Reemah and Anansi are in conversation with Fuoco, discussing nerve compression management in shibari, accompanied by a real-time example of how they addressed it during a tie.

Nerve compression is one of the most common risks in shibari and as your practice progresses to include more challenging ties and suspensions, it’s not so much a question of ‘if’ rather than ‘when’. That ‘when’ can range from every scenario, from labbing to performances to, yes, on set for a Shibari Study production. While things may not always go according to plan in ropes, what is essential is having a strategy for addressing and managing complications such as nerve compression when they do occur – here, Ms Reemah and her model Anansi demonstrate a masterclass in exactly that.

This course provides a thorough example of what it looks like when nerve issues do occur during a tie. Remember that rope is highly personal and what feels like an acceptable risk to some may not be an acceptable risk to others, and how some people mitigate or manage risks may not be an option in every situation or tying dynamic. The intention of this class is not to provide an example that must be imitated exactly but, rather, to show how it can be done. Throughout the conversation, Ms Reemah and Anansi explore what effective communication can look like when problems arise, discuss the various adjustments they tried to troubleshoot the issue, and reflect on how they managed the moment together.

This class is appropriate for all levels as an example of what effective action can look like in the case of nerve compression in ropes. While this can inspire you, always let your own context, experience and risk-profile guide you to take the action most appropriate for you.

title: Intro To Hashira
about:
In this series, Tamandua and his model Mie Neko present an intro to Hashira Shibari (tying on a vertical beam), highlighting some of the special considerations needed when learning this challenging technique, two options for anchor points on a vertical beam, and three tutorials with variations of floor-based positions.

The 'Perpendicular Anchor' and 'Vertical Anchor' videos demonstrate two anchor points: one making use of horizontal or perpendicular beams that extend from the top of the vertical beam and one that ties directly onto the vertical beam, meaning that your play can be as varied as your architecture.

As Hashira makes its debut on Shibari Study with this series, we begin with floor-based foundation ties suitable for practitioners of all levels but who are new to Hashira Shibari. In the 'Simple Hashira' tutorial, Tamandua demonstrates how just a crotch rope and wrist cuff can be utilized to create a basic yet beautiful tie as well as explaining some of the unique safety tips to keep in mind when tying on a vertical post.

The second Hashira tutorial, 'Ebi Hashira', marries the traditional ebi ('shrimp') shape with the sturdiness of the beam for a low semi-suspension that elevates the bottom’s legs for an exposing and sustainable final position. Watch through to the end for some fun ideas to make this tie extra playful!

For more practiced riggers, Tamandua’s 'Inverted Ebi' gives the classic ebi shape a more demanding twist with an upside-down and compressed semi-suspension that cinches the waist tightly to the beam. The final position will give an intense challenge to the model and focuses on vulnerability and exposure, making it ideal for engaging play. For expert level riggers with prior experience with tying on Hashira, you might try to elevate this one until the model is fully suspended.

title: Creating Balance
about:
In this Shibari tutorial, Docvale and Bänana discuss the influence of technique in rope, focusing on three areas where mindfully adjusting your approach can create better balance in your shibari practice.


As soon as you need to use force as a rigger, says Docvale, there’s probably a trick you’re missing that could make it simpler. Good riggers, he says, are lazy – they understand that the less complicated you make things and the less you force, the easier it will be to tie. This course is intended to help you bring intentionality into aspects of your rope practice where it’s easy to develop bad habits, and while the lessons covered in these classes may be tricky to implement at first, they will have a positive impact on your practice in the long run.


The first class focuses on the position and posture of rigger. In this tutorial, Docvale will discuss the pros and cons of different positions in terms of exertion, how dynamic they are, the level of stability they offer, and how impactful they are or what they communicate to the person being tied.


The second part of this course looks at tips and tricks for better rope handling, as this is an aspect of your practice that can both generate balance as well as create imbalance, particularly in partial and full suspensions. We all tie in a sequential way, says Docvale, but it’s good rope handling that gives our tying a sense of fluidity.


The final two classes focus on body manipulation with essential advice for how to use less force for greater results both when the person being tied is seated as well as when they are standing up. In these classes, Docvale discusses how too much superfluous movement can lead to imbalance and mixed messages while clear and intentional movement can effectively communicate intent and make for a better bondage practice.


This course is suitable for all levels and is recommended for anyone looking to refine the way they communicate through their tying.

These classes do not require a partner or even any previous tying experience, yet by the end of this series you’ll have the practical skills and knots needed to start having some fun with basic bedroom bondage and to begin putting what you’ve learnt into practice.

The double-column tie is such a fundamental knot and during this class Anna will explain exactly how it comes in handy, making it one of the easiest and most practical knots for play.

These classes will also give you all of the tools you need to follow Anna’s previous classes on self-tying for practice and pleasure with knots that are simple, fast to tie and even faster to untie.

No matter what your level of experience, these knots remain fundamental from absolute beginner to rope expert. Master these and you’ll create a solid foundation for your bondage practice.

title: Rope As A Breath Play Tool
about:
In this rope bondage course, Docvale discusses how to begin exploring breath play in ropes with his model Bänana.


For those starting out in shibari, there may be a tendency to think of breath play as involving choking, tying the neck or gags. However, as Docvale and Bänana detail in this six-part course, having an impact on someone’s ability to breathe can be achieved by strategic application of ropes far beyond the obvious. Starting from the basis of a two-rope TK, this course delves into psychology and physiology of breath play with tips and tricks for how to build up from a simple chest harness and increase intensity for (quite literally) breathtaking rope play. Watch the videos in order to learn how to manage and increase the psychological and physical intensity in tandem for safer and more effective breath play:


The ‘Intro' video offers an introduction to breath play and both what to expect from the course as well as what to expect from this type of play.


The second part of the course, ‘Progressivity & Semenawa’, looks at the Semenawa style of shibari and how it lends itself to the physical and emotional intensity of breath play.


In the third video, ‘Psychological Impact – TK2', Docvale and Bänana begin with a simple TK, exploring how even subtle compressions and adjustments to how you tie a TK can already begin to impact breathing.


From a two-rope TK, there are numerous options to build on and play further with the breath, with the fourth video – ‘Neck - Third Rope’ – focusing on how to utilize a third rope to begin experimenting with pressure around the neck.


In the fifth video, ‘Thorax – Fourth Rope’, a fourth rope is added as the focus shifts from constraining thoracic breathing to constraining abdominal breathing, beginning with a tight single-column tie around the waist.


This final video of this breath play course, ‘Belly and Pubis’ looks at tying the belly and below with two options for creating additional compression from below the waist.


Breath play is a powerful type of edge play, so it’s essential to keep in mind that while elements of this course may be applicable to your own practice, restricting a person’s breath can have a profound physical and psychological impact and is never without risk. It is essential for both you and your tying partner to understand these risks before attempting to recreate anything you see in these classes. If your skill set is not suitable to safely attempt this course, feel free to watch the class for inspiration but do not follow along.

In this series, you'll find a variety of common stretch positions. Each video is designed to help you understand what muscles are actually intended to stretch in various positions, and the ways in which flexibility limitations might show up in your rope practice. Use this as a starting point to develop greater body awareness in and out of rope, and as a tool to help you understand how to customize stretches to your own body in ways that still target the correct muscles.

In addition, you'll find the All About Shoulders videos. While these are not necessarily stretching videos, they are intended to expand your understanding of how shoulders work and draw your awareness to this joint, especially as it relates to determining what sort of harnesses work for you body.

This harness is a perfect alternative to the TK without shoulder pain. The low, crossed position of the arms in front of the body allows the hands and fingers to drop elegantly in a similar fashion to a high-hands TK.


In the two suspension videos Gestalta demonstrates this harness being used for two different full suspensions: a simple but challenging face-up and a more comfortable torsion that pairs the harness with her Willow Tie. It was both Kyle and Estella's first time being suspended and they both felt very comfortable in this harness!

title: Fast Hands | Slow Burn
about:
This playlist is part of our Rope Resolutions challenge to help make 2026 your knottiest year yet, so practice regularly this January to earn your streaks and win a prize. Find all of the details in our Community!

Experience prerequisites: Pre-requisites are in the title! Fast hands really matter here. You might opt to use old rope if you’re new to tying in this way, in case your bottom wants out right now. For bottoms, panic management skills are important if things start to feel overwhelming as well as the ability to register when something is approaching your edge with enough advanced notice that your rigger can act accordingly.

This playlist is all about challenging your hands before you challenge your tying partner – and trust us, there’ll be plenty of both. Drill your speed all month in preparation for a tie that is deceptively advanced. You might not put every drill to work in the final course (especially while you’re kneeling), but you’ll be glad to have invested in your rope handling skills. Sometimes a slow burn is only possible with fast hands. That’s definitely the case to feel confident and safe in hua hua’s dense rope.

Work through the videos in order until your hands feel like they’ve developed their own independent sentience – in other words, when the movements come fluidly, naturally and with no need to think it out as you tie.

Heads up: The final two ties are intense from a bottoming perspective. When you’re building up a tie as maximalist as this, there’s no space for uncertainty – the leg overlap class is an opportunity to taste test this style of tying for both parties.

title: Reverse TK
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Gigi demonstrates how to tie a Reverse TK on their model Cait.


Unlike many TKs, which can be difficult to sustain for long periods, particularly in suspensions, this arms-in-front ‘Reverse TK’ is designed for comfort.


In the first video, Gigi demonstrates how to tie the harness, detailing the ways in which it is engineered to be more sustainable for bottoms, from the frictions placed on the front of the harness to the third band for extra support. This harness is suitable for models of all body types and levels of flexibility, with its construction allowing for numerous options for loading, making it an ideal choice for bigger bodied bottoms wanting more support to stay in the air through transitions in suspensions.


In the second video, Gigi discusses how this tie can be loaded for suspensions, with three different options: in front for face-up suspensions, on the side, and on the back for face-downs.


The harness part of this tie is suitable for students of all levels, however, please only attempt to suspend from this harness if your skill set allows it and you have some prior suspension experience.

title: Active Bottoming For Suspension
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Fuoco and her model Gorgone discuss active bottoming in suspensions with examples of how more – or less – effort from the person being tied can influence their experience.

For many rope bottoms, learning about active bottoming can be an ‘a-ha!’ moment in their rope education as it’s a practice that enables them to better endure tough ties like suspensions and make their own adjustments to protect their bodies without relying entirely on the rigger. However, as Fuoco and Gorgone – both experienced bottoms and riggers – discuss in this class series, active bottoming is a spectrum that begins with even the subtlest of micro adjustments, and there are even times when passivity may be a better option.

Using three different suspensions as examples, they explore when active bottoming is necessary versus when there’s not much you can do for yourself, and how to tell the difference. As they explain, active bottoming shouldn’t be the thing that’s hardest but that which is most energy efficient. From the rigger perspective, they also demonstrate how observing your bottom’s adjustments can give you clues for how to offer them more support in your ties or make them more challenging…

This shibari tutorial series is suitable for both bottoms and riggers beginning to explore suspensions in rope. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own rope practice.

title: Suspension Session | Bottoming and Backbends
about:
Experience prerequisites: This course assumes that both bottom and top are comfortable with the technical elements of suspension and have a good track record of communicating through challenging moments on the floor and in the air. If both of you are quite new to suspension, you might not complete the final video and instead stick with exploring the two partial suspension options.

There’s plenty of shibari learning material out there to challenge the person doing the tying, but how about the person being tied? This playlist is all about bottoming challenge, for bottoms who love a tougher experience in ropes.

As Gorgone mentions in the final course, the sequence presented here is relatively simple to tie and quite demanding to be in. The videos we've selected to help you prepare for this course offer you opportunities to explore backbending over waist rope, so that you can get familiar with the sensation before building up to the most challenging version of the position in the final video.

We recommend using the Butterfly Harness, as shown in the final tutorial. If you struggle with backbends, consider using the full Butterfly Harness (with the connection between the upper and lower body on the front, as Gorgone discusses in the video), or for a deeper backbend, you can tie the harness as seen in final the video.

Remember that wanting a challenge should not equate going from zero to a hundred – and especially not in ropes. You’ve got a full month to work your way through this playlist, so take it slow – the more time you spend on developing your confidence, comfort and resilience in each class, the greater your chances of success.

title: Positioning Between Partners
about:
In this shibari course, hua hua teaches a series of classes exploring how positioning between partners can influence your ties and sessions, with input from her model Olivia.

Think ‘position’ in shibari and you’re likely to imagine it’s all about the model and the shapes achieved in the course of the tie. As hua hua explains, though, while we might think less often of how the rigger is positioned in response to the bottom, it can still greatly affect the mood and experience of your rope sessions. Before you even lay the first rope, your starting positions can begin to communicate intent, create a sense of vulnerability or dominance, and allow you to introduce more or less challenge early on.

In the first class, hua hua explains the benefits and drawbacks of beginning your sessions seated or starting them standing. As she says, starting seated can help establish a greater sense of ease and intimacy; standing offers more space and options to play with proximity.

In the second class, hua hua explores how the rigger’s positioning behind, beside or in front of the bottom can be used to enhance engagement, amplify power exchange, or simply be more or less practical for different types of play.

In the final class, two seated starting options for bottoms are compared: kneeling (or seiza position) and cross-legged (or agura).

This course is suitable – and enocouraged – for all levels, and will help you approach your tying sessions with greater awareness and intention.

title: Ebi-Zeme Variation
about:
In this class, Gestalta teaches a floor-based variation of Agura & Ebi Shibari with their model Aleks.

Modern Shibari refers to any crossed-leg sitting position as Agura Shibari. If the upper body is tied and forced close to the open legs, it is called Ebi Shibari (shrimp tie) or Ebi Seme (shrimp torment). The body being bent forward and the knees widely spread, the position resembles the body and tail of a prawn or shrimp.

Gestalta revisits this classic position inspired by an ancient method of torture, ebi-zeme (海老責め).

If kept for a long period of time, this position will heavily restrict the breathing and generate strong blood flow restrictions creating a burning sensation throughout the entire body. The increased stress created by the variations of leg position she explains and demonstrates in this class will make the effect significantly more immediate and efficient on flexible models.

title: Nerve Safety For Rope Bondage
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Cait teaches a six-part course on nerve injury and nerve safety in ropes with their model Gigi.

Nerve injuries are one of the most common injuries we see in rope bondage. As the connections between body and brain, damage to nerves can be debilitating, which is why risk-aware rope play is so essential. This multi-class series is focused not only on raising awareness about where the most common injuries occur but also on providing insights into how to lower the risk of nerve injuries and how to handle them when they do occur.

The first class offers an overview of the anatomy of a nerve and how to tell the difference between nerve damage and circulation loss.

In the second and third videos, Cait discusses the nerves of the upper and lower body respectively, with a special focus on those most commonly affected in rope bondage.

The fourth part of the course focuses on the mechanisms of nerve injuries, particularly with regard to compression and shearing injuries, which are most commonly seen in shibari.

The fifth class examines some of the known risk factors that might may increase your likelihood of nerve injury in ropes as well as how you can begin to mitigate some of those risks.

Finally, the last video offers invaluable advice on how to handle a nerve injury if it occurs.

This course is suitable for all levels with indispensable information for both riggers and rope bottoms alike. Whether you’re just starting out or looking to refresh your nerve knowledge, we advise you to keep coming back to this information throughout your practice.

Cait has prepared an amazing and highly comprehensive hand-out to supplement the content taught in their class. This is a complementary tool with the class. Click here to download and familiarize yourself extensively with its contents about nerves.

Please be aware that this is not professional medical advice. We encourage everyone to research this topic further and to always consult your primary care physician when in doubt.

about:
In this shibari class and demonstration, Tifereth explores techniques for physical rope on the ground with her model Irkalla.

One of Tifereth’s favorite ways of tying involves a very physical, hands-on approach on the ground. This technique is less about perfect knots and frictions (or any particular knots and frictions at all) and more about using your rope and body as a tool to press, pull and stretch with intention to push your tying partner to their happy limits.

In the first part of the course, Tifereth demonstrates how just a simple rope can be used to play with body manipulation and feelings of compression, exposure, and more. Her advice? Let go of the idea that you have to tie anything formal and approach from a place of playful exuberance.

In the demonstration video, Tifereth expands on the basic drill taught in the first part of the course, incorporating a slightly more structured approach with only one goal: to make Irkalla feel good, bound and contained in a position that she likes.

The techniques taught in this class can be incorporated into any practice, no matter your level of experience. As Tifereth explains, this is a “partner sport”, so be sure to check in with your tying partner as you set your intentions for this exercise. And do clear some space for play – you’re going to need it.

This is the first of three “Physical Rope” focused courses led by Tifereth. Keep an eye out for “Physical Rope: Partials” and “Physical Rope: Suspension” – coming soon.

title: You Know I'm Black, Right? (FREE)
about:
In this impactful discussion, Reemah, Anansi, and Lavender discuss being BIPOC in rope, rope spaces, and kink communities. They deep dive into the important nuances that exist at the intersectionalities of race and kink.

As Reemah, Anansi, and Lavender explain, for people of color, (particularly Black people) the experience of navigating kinky communities and playing with rope asks for greater awareness, intentionality, and inclusion as an active process. Topics covered range from understanding the importance of trauma-informed kink for BIPOC practitioners, and how to begin meaningful conversations about developing accessibility in rope, to how engaging in kink can be a type of reclamation. This insightful conversation explores how each facet of rope bondage and kink can be approached more mindfully to ensure that rope is truly inclusive of all people.

This class is suitable – and recommended – for all levels.

title: Geeking About The TK
about:
In this rope bondage tutorial, Gorgone will be going in-depth on a foundational shibari tie with their model Hongor – namely, the TK (takate kote) or box-tie.

As Gorgone explains, the TK is one harness that arguably involves almost all of the important ‘building blocks’ used in rope bondage, including things like tension, body mechanics, different frictions, nerve and placement safety – all thoughts and strategies that improve bondage skills.

The first class of this course is focused on the ‘theory’ of TKs. There are many different types of TKs and despite similarities across them, a one-size-fits-all approach does not apply. In this class, Gorgone will discuss variations in terms of style, priorities, needs, body types and more, summarizing everything useful they’ve learned in more than a decade of using this type of tie.

The second class in the course offers a practical positional study dedicated to skills and knowledge that are essential long before you even begin to place your ropes. With a focus primarily on body manipulation and body awareness, this class is key to understanding how to create a comfortable, safe and sustainable TK.

The third class offers a comprehensive demonstration of tying the TK, considerations that will come up as you tie as well as common mistakes people make when tying TKs and how to avoid them. Finally, Gorgone explores the pros and cons of adding a third rope to your TKs.

This class is suitable from beginner level up, though please only apply to your practice as far as your skill set will allow.

title: Fitness For Hyper Mobility (FREE)
about:
Designed with the needs of hyper-mobile students in mind, in this body care and movement class for bendy bottoms, Fuoco walks us through training and strengthening for hypermobility.

Hypermobility simply means that you have a greater range of motion in some or all of your joints than most people and you can extend them easily and painlessly beyond what most others can – it’s frequently referred to as being “double-jointed” (no double joints involved though).

But wait, that sounds perfect for Shibari? The reality is although you’ll often hear of bottoms thinking that they’re not flexible enough for ropes, the other side of the suppleness spectrum isn’t necessarily all neat party tricks and contortions either. Those models whose flexibility is beyond the normal range – who are hypermobile – can sometimes be more susceptible to injury and joint dislocation than their less bendy counterparts.

This class will help you develop joint stability to support your active bottoming skills and protect your body on the long run. If this style of work is new to you, expect it to be frustrating at first. For many people, this will be the first time that you've asked your body to work in this way, and it's likely that you'll spend several sessions feeling like you're not making any progress at all when, in fact, you're building the brain-body connection necessary to perform these exercises.

title: Gender Expanding TK
about:
In this rope bondage tutorial, Gorgone teaches adjustment techniques for gender-affirming TKs and chest harnesses with their model Miah.

Most patterns in shibari are designed for cisgender women, often highlighting the more ‘feminine’ characteristics with emphasis placed on the curves of the body.

However, this does not mean that harnesses or ties can’t be adapted to allow for gender euphoria. In this class, Gorgone details how rope placement in TKs and chest harness in particular are used to accentuate more aspects of the body that are commonly seen as 'feminine', as well as adjustments that can serve to feature deeper gender expansion in the ties.

This class is suitable for all levels, though please only apply to your practice as far as your skill set will allow. Additionally, it serves as an important reminder that shibari is not only for one type of body – it is for every body.

Lief and Icky have been performing together for the last four years and in that time have developed a style heavily influenced by their backgrounds in theatre, dance and the performing arts. At times tender, at times intentionally challenging, their suspension performance is an exercise in attunement, playing with pacing and intensity from the first moments to the very last.

title: Focus on Flow
about:
Experience prerequisites: You feel at home in our Getting Started category, specifically the Wrap it Up and Rope Handling and Flow courses.

Ready to move beyond the basics? In this playlist, you’ll be guided through a selection of classes curated to nurture an essential element for smoother tying: Focus On Flow.

Understanding frictions and knots is only one element of great tying in shibari. Flow is what lets you dance with the rope and your partner. It's the difference between tying first and then playing versus letting the play start the moment you pick up your rope.

Work through videos in order, moving on to a new technique only once you feel confident in the previous technique. Remember that even simple skills take time to develop, and you'll need both understanding and muscle memory for each component to feel successful when working with the final techniques.

From handling drills to harnesses and body manipulation, this playlist is all about easier and more intentional tying. This is also why we've chosen to culminate this playlist with some “one rope” offerings – this selection is not about a predetermined destination but, instead, is all about the journey.

title: Forward Tension
about:
In this step-by-step shibari class, Gorgone teaches the principle of forward tension with their model De’Jon.

Once you’ve mastered your basic anchoring knots to attach rope to the body, namely the Single-Column Tie and the Double-Column Tie, what to do with the rest of the rope? Everything we do with rope bondage is a combination of basic anchoring knots, wrapping and frictions. This class will introduce you to one of the fundamentals of rope bondage and one of the different ways you can wrap rope around the body – forward tension.

After learning the single-column and double-column ties, forward and reverse tension and a few simple closing options, you have enough tools to start playing around with rope in a creative way and explore free tying sensual floor-play. It can be that easy!

In this class, Anna Bones teaches a self-tying version of Shibari Study’s all-time most popular harness, the Butterfly Harness!

With over 1,500 hours of viewing time, the Butterfly Harness checks all the boxes: it’s multifunctional, aesthetically beautiful, comfortable to suspend in and suitable as a sustainable base for more complex – or torturous – ties. Plus, perhaps best of all, this arms-free pattern is entirely possible to self-tie!

While many students have successfully adapted this tie over the years, now – for the first time ever – the Butterfly Harness is being taught specifically for solo tying with plenty of valuable tips and tricks to upgrade your self-tying game.

about:
In this shibari class, Gorgone teaches their Infinity TK harness with their model Hongor.

This hybrid between a regular box-tie and the ever-popular Butterfly Harness is both pretty and practical, designed specifically to reduce direct pressure on the nerves of the lower arm while still offering the functionality and feel of a TK. This makes it ideal for models who are sensitive to nerve or circulation issues in the arms or who may be recovering from a previous injury.

During the class, Gorgone goes into detail about the pros and cons of the tie versus more conventional TKs, as well as offering two variations for keeping the top wrap in place.

title: Woven Heart Harness
about:
In this shibari class, Cait teaches the Woven Heart Harness with their model Gigi.


A modification of Gorgone’s popular Butterfly Harness, the Woven Heart Harness was engineered to prevent the issue of the waist rope sometimes slipping up towards the floating ribs. Functionality and form are beautifully (and quite literally) woven together in this tie, with the eye-catching woven pattern on the front both securing the lines in place and making for more comfortable face-down suspensions with a wider distribution of pressure.


Far from being suitable for face-downs alone, the Woven Heart Harness can be loaded for suspensions from the front, back or side with the second part of the class focusing on where and how to attach your suspension lines.


This shibari class is suitable for all levels from beginner up and models of all body types and flexibility levels. However, please keep your skill set in mind and only attempt to use it for suspensions if you already have some prior experience.

about:
In this bondage tutorial, Ropunawa teaches a fully suspended version of his intense Choker Tie with his model Freya.


Rounding off his Choker Tie-based series of classes, Ropunawa demonstrates how the powerful tie can be incorporated into a visually dramatic suspension. Though the shape looks drastic, much of its weight is spread between the Futomomo and waist line, making it surprisingly comfortable for models who like suspending off of these types of ties. However, it’s not without its technical demands: starting on the ground, it’s lifted almost all the way with a Futomomo, meaning you need to be aware of how to lift heavy parts of the body and best practice for suspension lines.


We’ve been building up to this breathtaking inversion with Ropunawa’s earlier Choker Tie classes – and for good reason. The Choker Tie is a challenge on its own, and the addition of suspension lines brings with it a new level of complexity that requires plenty of experience with both suspensions and this type of edge-play. If your skillset is not yet at a level to safely attempt this tie, feel free to watch the class for inspiration but please do not follow along.

In this beautiful demo session, Gestalta and their model Aleks present "Mayfly" - a performance piece they usually perform on stage for a live audience. Unlike our previous demo sessions, this sequence is not an improvised play session but a choreographed sequence.

A lot of the rope sequences designed for live performances tend to be fast paced, emphasising technical complexity and showcasing a lot of transitions in the air for maximum "wow" effect. Gestalta presents here a more humble and minimalistic choreography allowing the performers and their audience to fully experience and appreciate every moment leading to the final full suspension. The face-up position they chose for the climax of this show displays the body caught in between falling and floating, a poetic tribute to the paradoxical experience of Shibari.

Aside from giving you up-close-and-personal insights as to how their exploding Mayfly TK and Mayfly Suspension taught on this website are woven into play, this inspiration session also reveals the connection and dynamic created between rigger and bottom as Gestalta and Aleks move together through this simple but very poetic sequence.

about:
In this spellbinding shibari performance, hua hua and her rope partner Dantianshi demonstrate the connective power of one-rope play.

“‘Ipponnawa’ means ‘one rope’,” explains hua hua. “Beyond the literal meaning, ipponnawa is a concept in shibari that was developed by the late master Yukimura Haruki. With one rope, the primary focus of the play is in its attention to communication and the interaction between each other to guide the scene. With this minimalistic approach to tying, one must make the most of every inch of the rope, and be more mindful about where you place the ropes. Ipponnawa is a reminder that you do not need much to have a profound and powerful experience in ropes.”

Playing with sensation, pacing, and closeness and distance, the performance offers an intimate glimpse of how even just one rope can be used with intent and purpose for immersive rope scenes. The performance is followed by a feedback interview with hua hua and Dantianshi as they discuss their impressions of the session.

title: General Rope Safety (FREE)
about:
In this free shibari safety course, Lecia gives you a general overview of the most relevant aspects you should understand before starting your bondage practice. This includes information about different types of rope, cutting tools, anatomical knowledge – especially about nerves and nerve damage symptoms – but also consent and communication, self-reflection, psychological aspects and pain processing strategies.

Although this course aims to be as exact as possible, you might find varying viewpoints and information when doing your own research. This course does not aim to provide definitive answers or absolute truths about the topics covered, but rather to guide you and encourage you to consider and investigate further on all of these important safety topics.

With this course, we wish to help you better understand, evaluate and navigate the potential risks associated with shibari in order for you to enjoy safer and more satisfying experiences in or with ropes.

title: Choker Tie
about:
In this class, Ropunawa teaches his infamous Choker Tie with his model and partner Freya.


This advanced bondage class explores the incorporation of one of the most erogenous areas, the neck, for titillating sensations and how to utilise its sensitivity and vulnerability for deeper connection and intense power-exchange rope play.


While not playing with breathing itself, this tie does incorporate pressure on the arteries of the neck, so the tutorial includes plenty of essential information on how to tie the neck in a safer way, and how to approach the differences in intensity, practicality, and aesthetics.


The choker tie is a very powerful edge-play experience for both rigger and model but also very tricky to do right, so we insist that students do not try to reproduce this tie unless they have extensive prior experience both with this type of play. If your skill set is not suitable to safely attempt this tie, feel free to watch the class for inspiration but do not follow along.

title: Kinoko's Performance Theory
about:
In this insightful discussion, Kinoko expands on how he approaches shibari performances, where he finds his inspiration and how he views his role within the shibari community.

Rope bondage fans across the globe are familiar with Kinoko as an icon of the shibari world. Perhaps less familiar though are the thought processes and traditional art forms that, these days, play an influential role in Kinoko’s performances. From ikebana (the Japanese art of flower arranging) to Japanese calligraphy, Kinoko reveals how his appreciation for these art forms has informed his rope practice and performance philosophy.

In the second part, Kinoko shares his view on the intricate nature of connection within shibari and explores the complexities of maintaining respect for personal relationships.

If you loved this deep dive into Kinoko’s inspiration, conceptualization and creative process around his performances, make sure you don’t miss his captivating Traditional Performance with model hua hua.

title: Diamond Hip Harness
about:
In this rope bondage tutorial, Cait teaches their Diamond Back Hip Harness on their model Gigi.


Inspired by Anna Bones and Fred Hatt’s ‘Bones and Rope’ hip harness, Cait created this hip harness to give a little extra back support to larger bodied models. Where more minimalistic hip harness may not provide enough support, the Diamond Back Hip Harness is designed to be both comfortable and aesthetic, with a waist rope, thigh wraps and extra rope over the backside to make it supportive and sustainable for bigger models in suspensions.


In the first video, Cait demonstrates how to tie the harness itself, sharing their tips and tricks for controlling tension and placement when tying bigger bodied people.


In the second video, they demonstrate how to attach suspension lines for the harness, with important advice on how to spread the load to make the most of the harness’s supportive structure.


This shibari tutorial is suitable for intermediate students and models of all body types and flexibility levels. Please keep your skill set in mind and only attempt suspensions if you already have some experience.

title: Gorgone's Hip Harness
about:
GO TO GORGONE’S HIP HARNESS GUIDE

In this class, Gorgone teaches her original Hip Harness with her model Becky. Designed from a model's perspective, this Hip-Harness is very well suited for dynamic self-suspensions and partnered suspensions and transitions.

The original tie is particularly well suited for bottoms with more flexibility in the lower back and those who enjoy waist-loaded harnesses. The "wide front" variation demoed on her model Aja is designed to remove all pressure from the waist and lower back for bottoms who prefer hip-loaded harnesses.

The very compact frontal stem gives this harness a very balanced distribution of the load between the three supportive layers and makes it very resistant to dynamic movements in suspension. The placements and tensions are designed to make it as comfortable as possible for inversions and bridge poses.

In the suspension line video, Gorgone shows how to create a stable anchor point. In the Self Suspension class, she demonstrates exercises to help gain confidence and autonomy in a Hip-Harnesses.

The demo video is a straightforward version of the same tie without talking. It is useful to overview the harness before studying the tutorial or to refresh your memory after you have watched the tutorial with full explanations.

about:

In this step-by-step shibari class, Fred Hatt teaches a Hip Cuff tie with his model Briki.

Using only minimal rope and just two double-column ties – one of the first knots you’ll learn as a shibari beginner – Fred demonstrates how to effectively secure the arms to the thighs for a fun tie that still allows movement but immobilizes the hands and arms.

For those who don’t already know how to tie the basic knots used in these classes, you can learn the Single-Column Tie or Double-Column Tie in our Beginner Course. For those who do, any single-column tie of your choice can be used in this class.

title: One Rope Agura
about:
In this tutorial, Ropunawa teaches a suspendable one-rope cross-legged tie (Agura) with his partner and model Freya.

This minimalist cross-legged tie, which is highly inspired by Yagami Ren, makes the most out of one 8-meter rope to explore one of shibari’s most traditional – and, for many models, accessible – shapes. The tie can also be elevated off the floor for added intensity.

Don’t let the single rope fool you either. For advanced rope bondage practitioners, ‘stripping down’ your practice can open up new ways to play and explore. As Ropunawa explains, it’s a concept that even after many years of tying can show you that there’s still so much more to learn and discover.

title: Consent And Negotiation
about:
In this casual shibari-inspired discussion session, Ms. Reemah, Anansi and Lavender explore the ins, outs and absolute essentials of consent and negotiation.

Consent is the power of your ‘yes’ or your ‘no’, explains Ms. Reemah. Negotiation in ropes, on the other hand, goes into the nuances of ‘what’, ‘how’ and ‘when’. Both consent and negotiation are essential elements of every rope scene – whether you’re tying with someone new, learning at a shibari workshop or playing with a long-established tying partner.

In the course of this conversation, three experienced rope practitioners and occasional tying partners share an engaging discussion filled with both funny anecdotes and profound insights into what consent and negotiation may look and sound like in a real-life rope practice. From the early stages of vetting potential new rope partners to the concept of ‘continuous negotiation’ during tying to how we wrap up our play with aftercare, this deep dive into consent and negotiation is all about fostering safer, more responsible and more rewarding play in ropes.

This discussion is suitable – and encouraged – for all levels.

title: Wrap It Up
about:
In the previous section, you've learned the basic knots to begin a tie and attach the rope onto the body, now what to do with the rest of the rope? In this class, Gorgone teaches forward tension, reverse tension and different options to close the rope at the end of a tie.

Everything we do with rope bondage is a combination of basic anchoring knots, wrapping and frictions. This class will introduce you to the different ways you can wrap rope around the body in effective ways, before learning the most common frictions for more sophisticated patterns.

After learning the single-column and double-column ties, forward and reverse tension and a few simple closing options, you have enough tools to start playing around with rope in a creative way and explore free tying sensual floor play. It can be that easy!

title: Doll’s Bamboo Harness
about:
In this shibari class, Kissmedeadlydoll teaches two version of Doll’s Bamboo Harness, her suspendable chest and arm harness, with her models Cutebutdeadly and Mickael.

Incorporating the arms, chest and a length of bamboo, this harness is a great option to bind the arms for those looking for alternatives to box ties. Go more minimalist or build in a little more support – as Kissmedeadlydoll explains, it can be adapted depending on your bottom’s needs.

In the first video, Kissmedeadlydoll demonstrates the base pattern of the tie on Cutebutdeadly, followed by a third rope-inspired front lock-off variation.

The second class picks up with the base pattern taught in the first video now tied on Mickael, however, this time with a variation designed to offer more anchoring for the wraps. As Kissmedeadlydoll explains, this can be helpful for bottoms with more rounded shoulders and bigger bodies or for those who prefer more support.

The final video shows how to add a hanger to the back of the harness for suspension purposes. (While it can be loaded from the back or side, Kissmedeadlydoll says that most people prefer it from the back, but feel free to experiment if it’s within your skill set.)

As this harness is designed for suspension, this tutorial is aimed at advanced riggers and bottoms who already have some suspension experience. Less advanced levels may be able to tie along but please only attempt to use this tie in suspension if your skill set allows.

title: Patternless Futomomo
about:
In this step-by-step shibari tutorial, Fuoco teaches a Patternless Futomomo with her model Enna.


Unlike many other futomomos which rely on a more structured banded pattern to secure the calf to the thigh, this ‘patternless’ variation utilizes more irregular rope placement for a tie that not only looks different to other futomomos, it feels different. As Fuoco explains in the class, this tie is comfortable and great for rope bottoms who might struggle with the pressure on the shin of other banded futomomos. For riggers, taking a less structured approach is also an opportunity to learn to approach tying more intuitively.


This class is intended for beginner levels upward. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own practice.

title: Flying Lotus Suspension
about:
In this shibari class, Gorgone will teach you their Flying Lotus vertical suspension with their model Hongor.

Minimalistic, magical and, above all else, easy to execute, the Flying Lotus is a great suspension to practice collaborative tying. By lifting the model into a vertical cross-legged position in the air, the person being tied is comfortably able to take control of their own balance, making for a tie that feels more synergistic and relaxed for both model and rigger alike. It is, as Gorgone explains, a simple tie with a beautiful result.


Additionally, there are endless variations when it comes to upper body ties to combine it with, making it the perfect opportunity to figure out how to use levels and body mechanics together with your bottoming partner.


This class is suitable from intermediate level up, provided you already have some suspension experience. Please only apply the skills taught in this shibari class as far as your own practice and skill set will allow.

title: Kinoko’s Updated TK3
about:
In this step-by-step shibari course, Kinoko teaches an updated variation of his three-rope TK (takate kote) with his model hua hua.


Good tying is all about adaptation and development – finding what works… and then finding something that maybe works even better. Kinoko’s TK3 has undergone some tweaking, adapting and even simplifying since the early days of Shibari Study when it initially graced our screens as our very first Kinoko-taught tutorial and became a go-to TK for many. In this course, Kinoko not only teaches his modified version in detail, he also explains why, when it comes to safety, the very first knot you tie is also one of the most essential to perfect.


In the first video, Kinoko discusses the role of the hon-musubi or square knot. The knot used to secure the wrists in a TK, the focus of this class is understanding both why this tie is so important as well as how to tie it in such a way that it’s secure, compact and enhances the safety of your TK.


Once your hon-musubi is perfected, it’s time to learn the updated TK3. The second video offers a precise and thorough walk-through of how to tie this chest harness with detailed explanations of Kinoko’s techniques and reasoning. The result? A comfortable TK that’s designed for style, safety and sustainability in suspensions.


This class is suitable for intermediate levels and beyond. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own practice, particularly if you intend to utilize this tie suspensions.

about:
In this class, Gorgone teaches a few options to suspend the Cocoon Tie with their model Alma.

This surprising tie is very different from the usually highly engineered harnesses presented by Gorgone, offering beautiful old-school aesthetics and a very restrictive feeling. It can be used for floor play or suspension, and will be particularly appealing to those who enjoy playing with exposure and helplessness.

This tie can be easily modified to suit different bodies or aesthetics, however it can be quite unpredictable in the air and shouldn't be suspended without special attention and care for the possibility of nerve compression or slippage of the wraps over the shoulders.

We recommend experimenting with it in partial suspensions before attempting to suspend fully. You can also use a pulley to lift the whole body at once instead of going up by increments as demonstrated in the class.

title: The Ice Game: Tools For Pain Processing
about:
In this shibari skills class, Margherita and Shakti Bliss expand your toolbox for processing pain and mindfully navigating intense sensations with a chilly hands-on exercise: the Ice Game.

Ever noticed how you hold your breath when anticipating something difficult? Or sigh in relief at a good outcome? What about the deep-in-your-belly moans you let out in a hard tie or the way you find yourself unconsciously gripping onto something as you try to manage discomfort? As Margherita and Shakti explain, our bodies tend to know how to process intense sensations without instruction. This class is all about identifying and honing these tools for self-regulation for better use when we need them, in or out of ropes. And because your body needs time to absorb and digest these skills, don’t wait until your next rope session to practice: the Ice Game is the perfect low-stakes way to get started and a safe way to play with challenging sensations.

This class is suitable for all levels and roles. Whether you’re a rope bottom looking to exercise somatic skills or a top looking for insights into emotional processing, this is your chance to have some fun and take away essential tools in the process.

title: Agura Transition Sequence
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Bänana teaches an Agura Transition Sequence with her model Marion.‌

It’s a common misconception to think that suspension transition sequences have to be fast-moving, dynamic and energetic, which – if you prefer a slower, more deliberate pace when tying – can make them feel quite daunting. This, Bänana explains, was her own concern, until she started trying more transition sequences and discovered that taking a calmer, less hurried and more meticulous approach can be a good thing! Using a three-rope Agura Tie and a three-rope TK, Bänana demonstrates a shibari suspension sequence that progresses from an inverted torsion to a gyaku ebi position, before being inverted and compacted for a final ebi shape.

‌As Bänana emphasizes in the Conclusion video, it’s not about recreating the tie exactly step by step but rather about always thinking about the next step or position. It’s important to be precise, she explains, with a reminder that feedback from the person being tied can be very valuable tool for refining your tying in these challenging yet rewarding sequences.

This class is suitable for advanced practitioners with ample suspension experience recommended for both rigger and model. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own rope practice.‌

title: Agura Harness
about:
In this class, Fred Hatt teaches a suspendable Agura Harness with his model Briki.

Modern Shibari refers to any crossed-leg sitting position as Agura Shibari. For floor play, a simple version of this tie is sufficient but when used for suspensions a more stable structure is necessary. In this video, Fred shows how to tie the Agura with a lot of reinforcements and a solid stem allowing for various anchoring options.

In the suspension video, he demonstrates some of the many possible ways to suspend from this harness. We recommend going back to the ground between the different positions to give your model a rest as this is a fairly intense and challenging tie to be suspended from.

Please feel free to use a different upper-body tie as an alternative to the TK in order to reduce the risk of nerve injury. Recommended harnesses for safer Agura suspensions; Butterfly Harness, Xana Harness, Misungui Harness, Fisherman Harness.

For expert users who wish to spice things up and feel confident using more demanding upper-body structures, you can replace the TK with harnesses like the Neck Hug, Bunny Tie, Tengu or Teppo, for example. If you choose to increase the difficulty by using more challenging chest harnesses, we highly recommend to first experiment with partial suspensions before attempting to fully suspend.

title: Neko Harness
about:
In this class, Tamandua teaches the Neko Harness with his model Mie Neko.

More than just a beautiful hishi tie, this hands-free and beginner-friendly harness is built for sensation-play, all the way from the various pressure points to the stimulating (or threatening) crotch rope. Combine it with other arm ties taught on this site (e.g. Tamandua's Bunny Tie, Strappado, Bamboo Tengu and Teppo, Kinoko's Forearm Binder, Gorgone's Neck-hug or Ladder Tie) for a tie as multifaceted as the gem it’s named after.

This harness is presented here as a floor-play tie but there’s no reason it can’t be used as a suspension go-to if you remove the crotch rope and reinforce the back. We leave it to our most advanced users to figure out the few modifications that might be required to make this harness suspension-worthy and suitable for their partner's unique needs.

title: Dynamic Transitions
about:
In this shibari class, Gorgone will be teaching a Dynamic Transition Sequence with their model Vivian.

One for more advanced practitioners, this dynamic transition sequence may be challenging but it rewards experienced riggers and active bottoms with a suspension progression that’s both fun and engaging.


As Gorgone explains, the graduation of different positions offers some intended for “resting” and others that may be more intense or strenuous. For riggers, it’s essential that you be highly proficient and confident in terms of your upline management as spending too much time on uplines will impact your bottom’s safety and experience. This sequence also requires some active bottoming in order to help with transitions between positions, so is recommended for models who enjoy or are comfortable with this style of bottoming.


This class is aimed at advanced students with plenty of suspension experience only. As with all suspension transition tutorials on Shibari Study, please watch the class in full and familiarize yourself with the sequence before attempting to tie it yourself.

title: Duality Sequence
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky teach their Duality Sequence, an advanced rope suspension sequence that “takes a shape and turns it on its head”.

Using a TK, their version of the Booty Basket and a calf-binder, Lief and Icky demonstrate this progressive suspension flow that starts out with a torturous tippy-toes stand-up position and ends in a beautiful, inverted position. During the course of their step-by-step explanation, they explain their decision-making, including tying on a ring rather than bamboo, detail important safety considerations, and offer ideas for other shapes and transitions you can explore. As they explain, there are several variations of this challenging sequence that you can continue and grow with – what’s key is identifying what works for you and what doesn’t, and adapting from there.

This demanding sequence is aimed at riggers and bottoms with plenty of suspension experience. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own rope practice.

title: Infinity Reverse Prayer
about:
In this rope bondage tutorial, Gorgone teaches the Infinity Reverse Prayer Tie with their model Hongor.

A challenge for riggers and models alike, this extreme and eye-catching harness is a great tie for more experienced practitioners to play with increased intensity. The first part of the class details exactly how to tie the harness with important safety considerations to keep in mind – please watch through in full before you attempt this tie.

Once you’re well-practiced and ready for the next challenge, the Infinity Reverse Prayer Tie can also be incorporated into suspensions, with the second part of the class focused on where to place your suspension lines as well as where to avoid loading this already-demanding harness.

As Gorgone explains in the class, this harness needs to be tied a lot tighter than a regular TK in order to maintain the position of the hands together between the shoulder blades. Due to the strenuousness of this tie, its risk profile with regards to nerve damage, circulation loss and pain is heightened. Please be mindful that you may have to untie it sooner than you think.

This class is recommended for advanced riggers and models only and should only be attempted with models flexible enough to be in this position.

title: First Partials: Wrist Cuffs
about:
In this shibari course, TrueBlue and Margherita explore tying the wrists overhead, sharing both a step-by-step tutorial and a demonstration session for one of the first partial suspensions you may learn.

Partial suspensions – ties where part of the body is elevated by rope while other parts remain on the floor – are where you lay the groundwork for exploring suspension in ropes. Or whatever the opposite of groundwork is… It’s here that your rope practice takes flight, which is why it’s so important to get your first partials right. In this class, TrueBlue and Margherita discuss techniques for tying, lifting and loading the wrists as well as your options for locking off. They also offer important safety considerations for tying this sensitive part of the body. As Blue explains, by the time you utilize this tie in play, you should be well practiced in applying, creating uplines and locking them off as well as releasing and untying smoothly and efficiently.

In the first video, you’ll learn how to apply the wrist cuffs as well as load and lock off your upline.

In the second video, TrueBlue and Margherita demo this partial suspension in action, not as a tie-along but to inspire your own explorations.

This partial suspensions-focused course is aimed at intermediate learners who have spent time exploring rope and tension on the body and understand the circulation and nerve risks involved with beginning to play with suspensions.

title: The Raven
about:
In this class, Fred Hatt teaches The Raven, a bizarre and torturous shape for suspension play, with his model Mio.

This surprising and challenging position can be kept on the floor as a partial suspension or raised to a full suspension. As this is an intense tie meant to be short-lived in the air, it is recommended to use a pulley system in order to lift and lower your model quickly and easily.

The chest harness used by Fred in this demonstration can be replaced by any other comfortable hands-free harness of your choice (e.g. Butterfly Harness or Xana Harness).

Despite its seemingly simple look, this position requires a fairly advanced level of experience on both sides of the rope. The very minimalistic structure used for this suspension demands that each element is executed carefully and properly. We hope you enjoy this class and practice carefully!

title: Ankle Ties
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Gorgone teaches the ins and outs of ankle ties, from important considerations to get started all the way to a single ankle suspension.

Ankles are extremely delicate, meaning tying them improperly can fast become painful to the point of untying. In this series of ankle tie-focused classes, Gorgone covers techniques and applications that can make these sometimes-intimidating ties easier, safer and more sustainable.

The first class of this four-part series lays the groundwork for further exploring loading the ankles with useful advice for figuring out where pressure on the ankle may be less or more tolerable based on the anatomy of the person being tied.

In the second class, Gorgone details important preparations and adjustments that can be made before loading the tie.


The third-class is a more bottom-focused exploration of ankle ties, and looks at how the person being tied can actively influence their comfort in these ties and reduce pressure on this sensitive part of the body.


Finally, using all the information shared in the first three classes, the fourth class demonstrates a more sustainable, more beautiful and more comfortable single ankle suspension. (Please note: this suspension is categorically not recommended for self-suspension – only try inversions such as this with someone on hand to assist.)


While aspects of this course may be applicable from an intermediate level on, the single-ankle suspension is recommended for advanced practitioners with plenty of suspension experience only. Please always exercise caution when attempting this tie.

title: Kneeling Crotch Predicament
about:
In this shibari class, Kissmedeadlydoll teaches the Kneeling Crotch Predicament partial suspension with her model Cutebutdeadly.

A deviant take on DIY, this spicy predicament sequence opts for a piece of metal pipe as the newest addition to your shibari toolbox to inventively play with balance, stress, stimulation and suffering in a partial suspension. Of course, you can use bamboo too, but there’s something extra fun about hitting up your local hardware store to level up your rope scenes.

In the ‘Prepping The Pipe’ video, Kissmedeadlydoll demonstrates how to prepare your pipe or bamboo before you start your scene in order to minimize fiddling during play.

The session video follows, showcasing both the tie in action as well as step-by-step instructions on how to achieve this strenuous predicament. Watch for options for how to tie the upper body and head as well as how to build up the challenge one small-but-sadistic step at a time.

Finally, Kissmedeadlydoll and Cutebutdeadly offer a debrief and feedback session where they discuss their impressions of the tie. They also share ideas for how to make this challenging partial suspension predicament more painful or more pleasurable, depending on the sensations and emotions you want to bring into your scene.

Elements of this tie can be partially adjusted to fit your own preferences, however, due to its challenging nature, it’s best suited to riggers and bottoms with previous predicament experience. Remember that consent and negotiation are integral to all types of rope play, so check in regularly and remember that play can be stopped at any time.

title: Speed Tying Drills
about:
In this shibari course, Tifereth teaches a series of speed tying drills with her model Irkalla. These exercises are designed to help you tie more fluidly, smoothly and – of course – quickly.

Smooth, fast and fluid tying can bring more energy and playfulness into your rope scenes and, as Tifereth explains, is an essential skill for rope performances. Test your coordination and concentration – and you’ll come out a better rigger for it.

This course is divided into three classes – watch and drill each, pausing in between to take as much time as you need to practice each exercise until you’re able to repeat it consistently, smoothly and confidently:

1 On the Move – One of the most important elements of smoother, faster tying is learning to move both the rope and yourself. This standing drill will get you in the habit of moving your feet and your lines simultaneously, while maintaining tension in your rope.

2 Magnet Hands – Imagine your hands are two magnets repelling each other, keeping your hands as far apart from each other as possible as you move and tie, and you’ll have a good basis for smooth and speedy rope handling. The challenging part of this drill? Once you’ve figured out keeping your hands apart, it’s time to learn to move your body in opposite direction to your rope.

3 Bundling – Once you’ve got the hang of the first two techniques, move onto the final drill where Tifereth demonstrates a technique to bundle as you move that allows for better control of your rope ends. This drill is the most challenging but stick with it, and when you’re ready to level up, try changing directions.

These rope bondage drills are suitable for anyone wanting to improve and speed up their rope handling and flow. You don’t even need a partner – these can be practiced around a pole or pillar too. We recommend that everyone spend some time drilling these skills, no matter how advanced your practice.

title: Handling Drill For Better Frictions
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Fuoco explains the concept of ‘making rainbows’ in rope, with tips and pointers for how to avoid making rainbows but fold your rope instead for more efficient tying.

‌Oftentimes, better rope handling comes down to our most basic techniques and the good habits we’ve picked up along the way – or the bad ones we might not even realize are impacting our ties. In this beginner-friendly drills class, Fuoco focuses on ‘making rainbows’, a rope handling habit that can lead to uneven rope ends and less effective frictions. Then, using Munter hitches to demonstrate, she offers an alternative approach, folding the rope where it needs to turn, for better tie building.

This rope bondage course is suitable for beginner levels up and does not require a tying partner. We recommend that everyone spend some time drilling shibari fundamentals, no matter how advanced your practice.

title: Kinoko’s Maete Harness
about:
In this shibari course, Kinoko teaches the suspendable Maete harness with his model hua hua.

While behind-the-back box-ties and variations on the TK may be the more traditional options for a suspendable harness, placing the hands in front of the body can make for greater comfort and sustainability. Kinoko’s Maete tie offers a hands-front harness built for face-up suspensions with plenty of supportive wraps in the back and a stable and sturdy structure in the point for attaching your suspension line.

In the first class, Kinoko offers a step-by-step demonstration for how to tie the Maete harness.

In the second class, you’ll learn how to add a hip harness that will offer even more stability in the suspension to follow.

In the final class, Kinoko demonstrates how to suspend the tie, explaining how certain lines can be raised or lowered based on your model’s needs to increase sustainability.

This course is great for expanding your harness repertoire and for learners looking for alternative to TKs. However, please keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from these classes and only use this harness in suspension if that is already a part of your rope practice.

title: Tying Bigger Bodies
about:
In this four-part rope bondage tutorial series, tying partners Cait and Gigi discuss rope for bigger bodies.

There is very little representation of bigger bodies in bondage and, as a result, many misconceptions and negative stereotypes around tying bigger bodies. This course is designed to emphasize the fact that every body is unique and that rope is adaptable. As Cait and Gigi explain, it’s about knowing how to tie the person you intend to tie, about partnership (being able to communicate openly and being receptive to feedback) and about being able to modify ties to work for you.

In the intro video, Cait and Gigi go over some all-important safety considerations to take into account before starting with the rest of the course.


The next videos cover the topic of harness stability and comfort, with useful advice on how to approach tension and rope placement when tying bigger models, including a useful exercise you can incorporate into your rope practice for finding the best tension and placements in your ties.


Finally, Cait and Gigi offer their tips and tricks for getting bigger bodies into the air in suspensions.


While elements of this video series for tying bigger bodies can be beneficial for every level and any practice, please keep your skill set in mind and only attempt the suspension part of the course if you already have some prior experience.

As Lief and Icky explain in the intro to this series, floor-based performances might get less airtime than their suspension-focused counterparts but they are no less connective or evocative. In fact, rope scenes on the floor allow for easier risk mitigation and more accessible play without the need for advanced techniques or intimidating ties. In this dynamic session, they demonstrate how scenes on the floor can be both playful and impactful.

Before the session, they offer insights into how they negotiate their play as established rope partners with four years of tying together behind them. The session is followed by an intimate interview, in which they offer feedback and each discuss their impressions of the session.

title: One Rope Rodeo
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky share a labbing-for-better-rope game designed to help you use your rope more effectively: One Rope Rodeo.

Much as you don’t need a suspension point or advanced skills to start exploring fun and rewarding rope play, you don’t need a huge rope kit either. As Lief explains in this class, there are many ways to play with a single rope and to effectively use one rope to manipulate the whole body. One Rope Rodeo is a game that challenges you to make smarter and more efficient choices as a rope top and to think about placement, position and even out-of-the-box adaptations to make a single hank of rope go a long way...

This floor-based tying exercise is suitable for all levels, as long as you allow your own skill set to guide you. There are lots of follow-along patterns out there but it’s games like this that create a foundation for creative, flexible and engaging tying.

title: Forward Fold Predicament
about:
In this class, Tamandua teaches a standing predicament with his model Alma.

This simple yet highly effective predicament offers a delicious mix of pressure and fatigue-based stress. The legs tied into the chest will challenge the bottom's balance and force them to push on their toes to relieve the pressure.

Shifting weight onto the chest harness will relieve the waist but increase the compression of the chest area, rendering breathing more challenging. Vice versa, when shifting weight away from the chest, pressure on the waist will become more painful.


The tie itself is fairly simple to execute and is ideal for those who enjoy playing with "slow burn" positions, giving time to the predicament to build up slowly and become increasingly challenging and pleasurable. You can add accents such as hair rope or gag to add more sensations.


In this class Tam uses a TK (boxtie), but you can feel free to replace it with another chest harness that suits your preference and risk profile better.

title: Choker Tie | Partial Suspension
about:
In this bondage tutorial, RopuNawa teaches a partially suspended version of his infamous Choker Tie with his model Freya.


Using just a simple waistline, this class demonstrates how this powerful harness can be incorporated into a partial suspension. While the addition of the suspension line may not be technically complex, this is still a highly demanding tie, which can be stressful for the model both in terms of pain and restricted breathing. With this in mind, RopuNawa also offers essential guidance for what you can play with and what best to avoid in this already challenging position.


The Choker Tie has more than earned its reputation as one of Shibari Study’s most exciting ties, with the new addition of a partial suspension adding even greater intensity. Therefore, we need to stress that this tutorial is only suitable for riggers and models who have extensive prior experience with this type of edge-play. If your skill set is not yet at a level to safely attempt this tie, feel free to watch the class for inspiration but do not follow along.
