title: Coconut Rope
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky offer a deep dive into the risks and rewards of playing with coconut rope, as well as techniques for utilizing it on the floor or in suspensions.

Mean, scratchy, messy, difficult to handle and impossible to break in, coconut rope will shred your fingers, shed all over your floor and insult your mother. Of course, what makes coconut rope so challenging to tie with is also a large part of what makes it such a fun tool for sensation play in shibari – if you know how. In this series, Lief and Icky detail what to expect from this rough and unwieldy fiber, including the very real safety considerations for both bottoms and riggers, and how these should influence how you use and apply it.

In the first video, they offer advice for the basic handling of coconut rope, using a futomomo tie as an example for how to place it on the body, as well as sharing their tips for the kinds of applications coconut rope is and isn’t suitable for.

In the second video, they demonstrate how even just one hank of coconut rope can be used to create a compression chest harness, exploring both breath play and sensation play in one mean-but-minimalist tie.

In the third video, you’ll see how coconut rope can be used to create a tengu tie for more sadistic floor play.

In the final video, Lief and Icky offer insights for how coconut rope can be used in suspensions – not for load-bearing structures or uplines, but to add sensation and intensity under your other suspension-suited fibers.

This course offers guidance for how coconut rope can be used at every level of your rope practice. However, due to the risks involved, it’s important to be absolutely certain that playing with it falls within your risk profile as well as that of your tying partner/s. Start slow and always keep your skill set in mind.

title: Armbinders For Everyone
about:
HARNESS GUIDES: DIAMOND PATTERN, THICK STEM PATTERN

In this class, Fred Hatt teaches different ways to tie an Armbinder with his model Mio.

When tying an Armbinder (or Strappado), it is important to evaluate your partner's flexibility and preference so the tie is adapted to their unique needs. The position of the arms as well as the choice of pattern will vary accordingly. This class aims to give a better understanding of both body and rope mechanics in order to adapt the tie to each new partner and purpose.

Armbinders are challenging ties involving a higher risk of injury than most other harnesses. In this video, Fred explains some of the common sensitive areas and mistakes that could lead to injuries and how to better recognise or avoid them by making the right choices while applying the rope.

The first example is better suited for models with less flexibility, while the second example is better suited for more flexible models looking for a stricter Armbinder. The different technical approaches he presents can hopefully help you understand what type of structure will fit different bodies, and allow you to modify other patterns if needed.

title: Can You Get Out Of My Rope?
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky share a tension-filled rope game called ‘Can You Get Out of My Rope?’.

Tension is one of the most important elements of rope bondage but what exactly does this mean and what does good tension in ropes look (and feel) like? As Lief explains, one of the most common mistakes many riggers make early on in their rope journeys is tying too loosely. In this fun and beginner-friendly rope game, you can start developing a hands-on feeling for tying with proper tension with no knots, no frictions, only one rope, and the challenge: can you get out of my rope?

This exercise is both suitable and recommended for beginners. With both a ‘simple’ and a ‘harder’ version demonstrated, try the variation that best suits your practice until, well, tension comes easy.

title: Tenshi Harness
about:
GO TO TENSHI HARNESS GUIDE

In this shibari tutorial, Tifereth teaches her chest-free Tenshi Harness together with her models Irkalla, Fuoco and Mickael.

Tifereth first developed the Tenshi Harness back in 2016, and since then it’s taken off as a versatile upper body harness that avoids some of the sustainability challenges associated with harnesses that incorporate ropes across the chest. This course will teach you everything you need to know about the Tenshi: from how it was developed and got its angel-inspired name to harness construction, safety, and how to tailor it to different body types, as well as how to attach uplines and use it in space.

The first part of the course offers a step-by-step demonstration on how to build the Tenshi, with important considerations for tensioning as well as tips for rope bottoms on how to help (or, rather, not help) to ensure correct rope placement.

The ‘Tenshi Safety’ video explores considerations for risk-reduction as you tie, with special attention given to movement, body manipulation, tension and line placement, and how they may impact the nerves of the upper and lower arms.

In the ‘Tailoring the Tenshi’, Tifereth demonstrates subtle but important adjustments for tweaking the tie to better suit different anatomies and levels of mobility.

Finally, the ‘Suspension Lines’ video explores where and how to attach suspension lines to the Tenshi for more experienced practitioners who are ready to take it into the air.

This course is great for expanding your harness repertoire and for learners looking for alternative to TKs. However, please keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from these classes and only use this harness in suspension if that is already a part of your rope practice.

title: Tying Slowly
about:
In this three-part shibari course, hua hua discusses the many benefits of tying slowly with her model Olivia.

Impactful rope bondage is about more than just technical skill. Rope handling, pacing, being able to read your rope partner’s reactions and being able to respond accordingly are important elements that can all affect the flow and feel of a scene. In this class, hua hua makes a case for slowing down when you tie – to make space for observing, for ongoing consent, for finding inspiration, for processing and for being able to identify when a tie may need to be modified or changed – and offers suggestions of when and where to pause. As hua hua explains, intentionally slowing your pace is not only a powerful tool for creating a more intense mood, it also helps to mitigate some of the communication and safety issues that may arise from tying in a rush.


This class is applicable to all levels, from beginner to expert. Every practice can benefit from a more intentional and nuanced approach to tying; how and where you apply it will depend on your own skill set, so remain mindful of where you are at and allow this class to inspire you accordingly.

title: Basic Knots By Gorgone
about:
In this class, Gorgone teaches the Single Column Tie and Double Column Tie, explains their different functions and when to use one to the other.

The only time full knots are used in shibari is to start a tie and create an anchor point onto a limb or a body part, for this we use two basic ties called Single Column Tie (SCT) and Double Column Tie (DCT). These knots are the most basic but also most important ones, they should be practiced until your hands are faster than your brain.

One of the most important thing when tying someone else is to make them feel that you can tie those first knots quickly and confidently so they can let go and enjoy. Ideally you should be able to do these basic ties without looking at your hands, so you can rely on muscle memory and focus on your partner rather than your knots.

If applied creatively to the body, these two knots and a few simple rope wrappings and shibari frictions are enough to create beautiful and playful ties!

title: Drills For Self-Tying Behind Your Back
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Kissmedeadlydoll shares a series of exercises and drills for self-tying behind your back with her model… herself!

As Kissmedeadlydoll explains, knowing how to tie behind your back is helpful if you’re working towards tying harnesses for self-suspensions. However, where you’ve got your eyes to guide you when tying a partner, now you have to rely on your hands, fingers and sense of your rope in space. Tying behind your back requires mobility, dexterity and plenty of practice connecting your brain to your fingers, so this is where drilling key skills until your fingers act as your “eyes” is essential for developing fluidity and confidence. The drills taught in this course will help you learn to feel your way through tying some common frictions and hitches behind your back, including:

1 Half-hitches

2 X-frictions

3 Half Moons and L Frictions

4 Collapsed hangers

Watch and drill each, pausing in between to take as much time as you need to practice each exercise until you’re able to repeat it consistently, smoothly and confidently. This course is perfect for anyone interested in self-tying, as well as anyone looking to improve their tying coordination and proficiency.

about:
In this class, Gorgone teaches various applications of crotch rope (also called matanawa) with their model Alma.

Crotch rope can be tied in several different ways and, depending on your intention, used to create very different effects. These range from being utilized for purely decorative and aesthetic purposes to being used to apply pressure and erotic stimulation, and also as accents for predicaments and torture ties.

This class is designed to take a closer look at this type of tie with practical advice for how to adapt the ties for different anatomies and – of course – how they can be used to explore the spectrum of sensation from pleasure to pain.

Before beginning to experiment with crotch rope, remember your fundamentals of negotiation and enthusiastic consent. Decide in advance how you will use this type of tie and always make sure your partner is comfortable with it before applying ropes in intimate areas.

title: Exposure And Closure
about:
In this shibari course, Lief and Icky explore vulnerability through both exposure and closure in rope. They offer lectures, structured exercises, and demonstrations of these concepts to help you understand how to bring intensity and intimacy to your own rope scenes.

Playing with vulnerability is a powerful tool for heightening emotion in ropes. As Lief and Icky explain, this series of classes is all about exploring the ins and outs of physical and psychological exposure in rope. The course is designed to offer an intentional framework for navigating this exciting – and often challenging – type of play, beginning with a lecture focused on defining vulnerability and accessible ways to get there in ropes, incrementally building up to more demanding scenes.

Following the lecture, Lief and Icky demonstrate three exercises that use the principles of exposure and closure to start building up your vulnerability-centered scenes: a ‘Naughty, Nice & Needs’ exercise that offers a practical and fun way of discussing desires; an ‘Ugly Vs. Pretty Rope’ demo that expands on what both ‘naughty’ and ‘nice’ could look like; and a ‘Closure’ exercise focused on untying and ‘putting the person in ropes together after we’ve taken them apart’.

Finally, in the Floor Demo, Lief and Icky put all these elements together for a beautifully connective rope scene that balances demand and reward, surrender and trust, and plays with the full and potent spectrum between exposure and closure.

For some fun-but-effective ties to inspire you to start exploring exposure and closure in your own practice, check out Fred Hatt’s Mini Arm Ties.

title: Easy Floor Play
about:
This playlist is part of our Rope Resolutions challenge to help make 2026 your knottiest year yet, so practice regularly this January to earn your streaks and win a prize. Find all of the details in our Community!

Experience prerequisites: Basic knots and frictions – this playlist is all about taking those foundational beginner shibari techniques and allowing you to play with them.

In this beginner-friendly playlist, you’ll learn how to start elevating early skills from “practice” to “play” with simple floor-based techniques focused on rope handling and flow. You’ll be able to put your abilities to the test with some of our favorite floor harnesses, curated to help you create your own floor flow sequence!

When we think of transitions on rope – moving between positions and ties in a coordinated and intentional way during your session – we tend to think of advanced suspensions. However, floor play can be as much about transitions as suspension. Being able to tie and untie quickly and move a partner through various positions can be the difference between “tying someone up” and “doing rope”. It’s here that you begin to discover the real magic of rope, where there is no final position and the journey is the destination.

Work through the videos in order and pay attention to how drilling your rope handling first makes tying harnesses all the more fluid. Make time to explore how it feels to mix and match these upper and lower body ties, find your favorite combinations, and then get collaborative about how you can move between positions. This is all about spending less time fiddling and more time connecting with your partner.

title: Drills For Single-Column Ties
about:
In this shibari tutorial series, Fuoco teaches a series of drill exercises to help you practice and perfect single-column ties.

The single-column tie (SCT) is one of the first ties anyone learning shibari will encounter. As one of the fundamental building blocks of your rope practice right from the get-go, it’s essential not to dismiss the humble SCT as basic or unimportant. As Fuoco explains in this course, even the best and most advanced riggers dedicate themselves to making their single-column ties smoother, faster and cleaner. These exercises are designed to help you do the same, by focusing some time and energy into constructing better single-column ties.

This shibari course is divided into five videos – watch and drill each, pausing in between to take as much time as you need to practice each exercise until you’re able to repeat it consistently smoothly and confidently:

1 Building the Wrap ­– tips and tricks for more efficient cuff construction.

2 Constructing the Loop – paying attention to how you fold your rope.


3 Theory and Locking the Cuff – understanding how the Somerville bowline works.


4 Switching Hands – okay, now learn how to do it all with your non-dominant hand taking the lead…


5 Switching Directions – once you’ve mastered switching hands, further develop your handling by tying the cuff in the other direction.


This rope bondage course is suitable for beginner levels up. We recommend that everyone spend some time drilling shibari fundamentals, no matter how advanced your practice.

In this beginner-friendly playlist, you’ll be guided through all the skills needed to tie one of your first rope harnesses: the Neck Hug. Requiring just a few basic knots and frictions as well as some simple techniques, this is the ideal place to start honing and applying your new shibari know-how.

Work through videos in order, moving on to a new technique only once you feel confident in the previous technique. Remember that even simple skills take time to develop, and you'll need both understanding and muscle memory for each component to feel successful when tying the harness. Learn and “lab” the harness before playing with it.

Heads up: Learning can be slow going, so let your tying partners test the position first without rope to make sure it's comfortable enough for them to be tied there for a sustained time.

about:
In this step-by-step shibari course, Fred Hatt teaches four simple arm ties – using only single- and double-column ties and minimal rope – with his model Briki.

In the Elbow Cuff class, the arms are bound together at the elbows with the hands up towards the face – a great starting point for building on the tie but also perfect for playing with on its own.

The Tengu class teaches a simplified version of the classic Tengu tie, which creates a vulnerable and chest opening position without putting too much rope on the body itself.

about:
In this step-by-step shibari tutorial, Bänana teaches a Self-Hug partial suspension with her model Fred.

A classic and minimalistic position with the arms wrapped around the backs of the legs, this compact semi-suspension is achieved without the use of a chest harness. Instead, it uses a straightforward Basket Tie and lacing up the lower part of the legs to achieve a playful partial. However, despite not involving too many technical elements, this tie is great for challenging your rope- and body-handling skills. In this class, Bänana demonstrates exactly what you’ll need to keep in mind to achieve the final ‘self-hug’ position as effectively and safely as possible.


This class is suitable for intermediate levels and beyond. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own practice, particularly if you intend to utilize this tie in semi-suspensions.

title: Gyaku Ebi | Hog Tie
about:
In this class, Gorgone teaches a hogtie form or "Gyaku Ebi" (meaning inverted shrimp in Japanese) with her model Joann. The hogtie is a common method of Shibari restraining all four limbs together behind the body, rendering the subject immobile and totally helpless.

The course is divided into separate classes introducing three variations of this tie for floorplay, partial suspensions and a full transition sequence. In these classes, Gorgone uses her TK3 and Fast Leg-Tie but other alternatives can be used instead.

The floor-based variation is suitable for intermediate level or beginners by replacing the TK with a safer and more simple chest harness. The partial variation is suitable for intermediate-advanced levels.

The transition sequence should be performed by expert practitioners only. It is a challenging transition sequence, combining elements of old-school and modern suspension style.

title: Mayfly TK
about:
In this class, Gestalta teaches two versions of their Mayfly TK with their model Aleks.

Both variations offer the basic functionality of a traditional TK but with an interesting twist. By keeping the arms down at the side of the body instead of in the usual behind-the-back 'box-tie' position of a standard TK, the stress of internal rotation is taken out of the shoulders, making for a more comfortable and sustainable tie.

In suspension, this harness leaves the arms draped around the body for a poetic and less traditional aesthetic. It’s an ideal option for bottoms who are comfortable with pressure on their arms but have limited flexibility in their shoulders.

The 'Original' version of the tie is the more structured of the two and is recommended for transitions or extended time periods.

Where the first variation offers stability and practicality, the second delivers the drama, with a dynamic 'exploding' take on the harness that comes off easily in the air, making it a thrilling tie for both performance and play. You can see it used in action in the Mayfly Session.

title: Lavender Harness

In this shibari tutorial, Ms Reemah teaches her suspendable Lavender Harness with her model Lavender.

The Lavender Harness is the little harness that could – unassuming at first, but with even more potential than its seemingly simple structure may immediately reveal. As Ms Reemah and Lavender explain, the harness was first developed out of a desire to avoid box-ties. The result was a simplified arm binder/TK hybrid that goes big on ease of construction and utility, and minimalist on just about everything else.

In the first part of the course, Ms Reemah shares step-by-step instructions for how to construct the Lavender Harness, including important tips for perfecting your tension – the key ingredient for this tie to work exactly as intended.

In the second part of the course, Ms Reemah expands on just how versatile this harness is in suspensions, demonstrating where it can be loaded from the back, front and sides.

This shibari course is suitable for tying pairs expanding their harness repertoires and looking for alternatives to TKs that prioritize comfort and functionality. Please only attempt the suspension part of the class if you already have some suspension experience.

title: Context & Characteristics
about:
In this rope bondage class, Anna Bones delves deeper into the context and characteristics that inform what we call ‘shibari’.

What do we mean when we speak about ‘shibari’ and how does this differ from other types of bondage? And beyond the words we use, how can rope itself be used as a tool to communicate our intent? This theoretical class is the perfect starting point to understand why we tie the way we tie, why we use the tools we use, and how these – and not the ‘end result’ of a specific harness or pattern – are some of the most rewarding aspects of the practice.

This class is aimed at beginners and those with an interesting in bondage looking to start expanding their understanding of the whys and the hows of shibari.

title: Dense Rope
about:
In this shibari course, hua hua teaches an advanced style of heavy rope bondage she calls Dense Rope with her model Dantianshi.

Heavy bondage is all about intentionally creating intensely restrictive sensations. In ropes, this can mean building up highly compressive ties by applying plenty of rope to the body – hence, ‘dense’ rope. As hua hua explains, this type of bondage is great for people who enjoy the sensations of swaddling or mummification. However, because so much rope is used and the tie takes so long to build, tension control is essential, as is understanding the risks of being in ropes for a significant period of time.

In the first class, hua hua demonstrates how to start this full-body bondage, working up from the feet to the shoulders (or even applying face rope, if desired). As she ties, hua hua also explains the best technique and approach for building up this challenging tie, including tips and tricks for where to place rope joins and how to approach spacing and tension to achieve that maximalist effect. After all, the way you build the tie is key to keeping things as sustainable as possible for as long as possible.

In the second class, the upper body is tied too. As hua hua explains, as you begin to build on the chest, it becomes harder for the person in ropes to breathe comfortably, while the legs are able to withstand more pressure for longer periods. Be mindful with how you approach this tie as it takes a long time to tie and to untie.

This Dense Rope style is recommended for advanced riggers and bottoms only. This type of play should be approached with intention and awareness of the risks involved.

title: Self-Suspension Challenge
about:
This playlist is part of our Rope Resolutions challenge to help make 2026 your knottiest year yet, so practice regularly this January to earn your streaks and win a prize. Find all of the details in our Community!

Experience prerequisites: Experience with simple/static self-suspensions. Please have a spotter with you (ideally someone who understands how to help you untie, but at minimum, someone with whom you've discussed an emergency descent plan).

This playlist is for our self-suspenders! The final video is not a purely instructional course on the entire sequence, but rather a presentation of concepts that you can absolutely recreate as is or expand on as you like.

We've included Kissmedeadlydoll’s self-suspension chest harness here, but any arms-free suspendable harness will do. We’ve also included two hip harnesses, both fairly simple to self-tie, for you to choose from if you'd like to follow along precisely with the final set of videos.

Remember that even with all the necessary knowledge and understanding to follow along, endurance can only be built up over time – you have all of January to work through this playlist, so use it. Once you’re recreating what you see in the demo videos, consider tying just the first demo in the beginning until that is comfortable. From there, you can begin adding shape exploration until that’s comfortable, and so on. Gradually, you’ll build enough endurance to follow along.

Heads up: Please take note of Kissmedeadlydoll's suspension setup, with a suspension ring and carabiner. Four lines on a ring are likely to overlap or get jammed, so please start with a rigging setup that’s appropriate for what you intend to do.

title: Active Bottoming
about:
In this series you'll find different videos, including movement-in-rope exercises suited to lab-style explorations and physical aftercare, designed to help you:

  • Understand what "active bottoming" might entail in these common positions of facedown and torsion suspensions.

  • Develop a sense of when your body is safer/less safe in these positions.

  • Understand what skills you can develop or utilize, in some situations, to protect the health of your body in these strenuous positions (during and after a session).

  • Help riggers to have a clearer sense of when a body is in a more or less compromised and challenging position in these types of suspensions.

  • Help riggers to develop a clearer sense of how to balance stressful positions and put their bottoms into easier or harder variations of these positions.

The point is not that all of your suspension experiences here on out should achieve these sensations of balance and alignment. Rather these are exercises intended to build body awareness. You might find that they help you understand what small adjustments you can ask for to make positions more sustainable or give you a better sense of what micro-adjustments you can make yourself.

For the Facedown Exploration video:

  • Explore first how you tend to be lifted into the position, and then how it feels to be lifted into the position maintaining a more aligned and engaged open-hip position.

  • Explore pelvic tilt and low back release, in proper alignment, at various levels, noticing when these subtle movements are more/less accessible to you.

  • If possible, attempt this on both a ring and bamboo. If bamboo is not available, explore the difference between being very close to the ring (short lines and wide angle) and very close to the floor (long lines and small angle).

  • Finally, notice if it's possible for you to both be in an aligned hip position and in a balanced facedown shape. Some folks with lots of tightness in this position in their hips might not be able to maintain alignment *and* be lifted into a balanced position (such that the weight of the torso is evenly/comfortably distributed between top and bottom wraps).

Please feel free to use any other harness as an alternative to the TK while practicing these exercises if it is safer and more comfortable for you or your partner.

title: Connective Uplines
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky present some fun strategies to use suspension uplines to connect more with your partners during rope scenes.

Once you already have plenty of shibari suspension experience, how can you make your scenes as much about connecting with the person in your ropes as it is about tying them well? As Lief and Icky explain, once you already have a good level of technical proficiency when it comes to tying uplines, you can start using those uplines for more connective tying.

This shibari course is divided into five parts, the first video detailing safety consideration for risk mitigation when you start playing with advanced suspension techniques, while the second offers step-by-step instructions for tying Lief and Icky’s favorite bottom lock-off. The next three classes each look at different ways in which your suspension uplines can do double duty, enhancing how you connect with your bottom. These include using extra upline to incorporate hair or mouth rope, combining uplines to create more compression in your suspension shapes and using extra upline to create lift or support in other areas of the tie. Finally, Lief and Icky demonstrate a suspension using all three techniques for a comprehensive example of how they can be used in play.

This shibari class series is aimed at riggers and bottoms who have studied and practiced secure uplines and feel confident enough to start adding a new element of challenge. As Lief and Icky explain, this type of play can add more risk as it adds extra time to your suspensions and may incorporate delicate parts of the body. They recommend beginning to explore these techniques in partial suspensions first. Allow this course to inspire and guide you only as far as your skill set will allow.

title: Suspension Challenge: Duality Sequence
about:
This playlist is part of our Rope Resolutions challenge to help make 2026 your knottiest year yet, so practice regularly this January to earn your streaks and win a prize. Find all of the details in our Community!

Experience prerequisites: You need plenty of suspension experience for this one. Don't work through the whole sequence until you've labbed each harness (bottom and top) and can tie each harness from memory without referencing the videos.

This playlist is a follow-along suspension sequence that’s ideal for exploring different shapes and transitions as well as gaining experience adapting the tie to better suit your needs each time you try it. We’ve collected all of the harnesses you’ll need to follow along, including a couple of box ties for you to lab and pick from. If you have a box tie you like, you can of course use it. You could also try this out with an arms-front harness or other upper body harness. The final position is a heavy torsion that will definitely behave differently from one harness to another. Very rarely do we get to just learn and copy a sequence out of the box – almost all learning at this level requires some labbing and adaptation and some of what you’ll learn in this playlist is to think critically about what the impact might be of any adaptations you make.

Heads up: Just as you learn the steps of tying a harness in order through repetition and mimicry before you start to make changes, it can be helpful to learn whole sequences this way too before making them your own. So try to start with minimally impactful changes as you get comfortable, but feel free to eventually take detours and make this sequence your own!

title: Solo And Partnered Stretching
about:
In this body conditioning for shibari tutorial, Ms Reemah and her model Lavender demonstrate a series of solo and assisted stretching exercises.

It’s time to set aside your ropes and explore an entirely different take on ‘working out the kinks’ with two stretching tutorials designed for before and after your rope sessions. As Ms Reemah explains, while there’s no such thing as risk-free shibari, proper stretching and body care can help mitigate some of the physical risks of the practice and even help you connect more deeply with your tying partner (or yourself). With one class focused on solo stretching for riggers and one on partnered stretching for bottoms, giving care and attention to the muscle groups most used in rope can become an integral part of your scenes.

In the first class, Ms Reemah discusses the often-overlooked topic of stretching and conditioning for riggers. Offering examples of stretches she likes to do before and after rope sessions, she focuses on the hands, fingers and wrists, and – for safer lifting – the hips, legs and thighs.

In the second class, Ms Reemah and Lavender demonstrate how stretching can be incorporated into aftercare after your rope sessions. As well as gently addressing any body strain or tension that may have arisen maintaining challenging positions, this is an opportunity for rope partners to reconnect and decompress together post-play.

This shibari tutorial course is appropriate for all levels. As Ms Reemah advises, do what your body can do – these exercises are not intended to be followed exactly but rather to give you an idea of how to target some areas frequently employed in rope. Each body is different, so meet yours where it’s at mindfully in order to avoid injury.

title: Bottom Led Suspension
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Icky and their tying partner Lief share another one of their labbing-for-better-rope games with a fun Bottom Led Suspension exercise.

Much like just about every other element of shibari, communication takes practice – we drill certain ties and frictions, so why not another essential tying skill: asking for what we need. As Lief and Icky explain, communicating efficiently and effectively about desires and needs while in rope is a critical skill for bottoms but can be difficult when processing challenging feelings or sensations, particularly in suspensions. This engaging exercise allows both the person doing the tying and the person being tied to make decisions about the eventual suspension, creating an intentional space where the only ‘goal’ is being able to express exactly what we need to make our ties feel safer, more sustainable or simply more rewarding.

This exercise is best suited for riggers and rope bottoms with suspension experience, always allowing your own skill set to guide you. If you prefer to play on the floor, feel free to adapt the game to best suit your practice. The goal here is improving your communication and that starts with meeting yourself and your tying partner wherever you’re at in your shibari journey.

title: Lacing Forearm Binder Partial Suspension
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Bänana teaches a Lacing Forearm Binder Partial Suspension with her model Marion.

Many of the suspensions we see in shibari rely on chest harnesses to bind the arms and upper body. But does that mean we need rope on the chest? Not necessarily. As Bänana demonstrates in this floor-level partial suspension, there are creative ways to bind the hands and suspend the upper body without using any rope on the chest. While tying this way might be beneficial or even necessary for some, excluding the chest also comes with its own challenges, says Bänana, and will require some adjustments and adaptations, particularly in terms of movement and body handling.

In the first class, Bänana demonstrates how to tie the lacing forearm binder, so as to avoid slipping and create a tie stable enough to attach a suspension line. Importantly, she also speaks about blood circulation and nerves, detailing sensations to expect and risk areas to avoid for safer, more risk-aware tying.

In the second class, Bänana combines the lacing forearm binder taught in the first video with a futomomo to begin exploring a partial suspension. Offering advice for how to gradually lift and compact elements of the tie, Bänana explains that once you understand the techniques taught in this class, there are plenty of possibilities for utilizing these two harnesses together for partial suspensions.

This shibari tutorial is suitable for intermediate and advanced students who already have some suspension and upline handling experience. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own rope practice.

title: Breaking Patterns Game
about:
In this shibari class, Kissmedeadlydoll teaches the Breaking Patterns Game with her model Cutebutdeadly – an improvisational tying-with-a-twist exercise to play your way out of ropey ruts.

If you frequently find yourself repeating the same sequences in rope or struggling to discover new shapes in partial suspensions, Kissmedeadlydoll has got a game for you. Created for rope students already comfortable with suspensions and body manipulation, the Breaking Patterns Game adopts a “fuck-around-and-find-out” attitude to encourage you to explore new and different options as you tie. Play this game frequently and remember to “deny yourself access to the first choice you would make”.

In the first part of this course, Kissmedeadlydoll highlights some important rules and considerations for the game. This includes how to start and how to progress, disregarding your Choice A and maybe even Choice B to introduce more experimentation to your rope.

In the next two videos, ‘Building the first shape’ and ‘Building the second shape’, Kissmedeadlydoll offers an unpractised and unplanned demonstration of how this off-the-cuff-tying game works and the very different results you can achieve each time you play. She also explains how to play “what if” before adding rope to the body, a fun technique for exploration that doesn’t limit your potential for new shapes.

Finally, Kissmedeadlydoll and Cutebutdeadly share a debrief and feedback session. After all, this game is an opportunity for both riggers and bottoms, to make new shapes and to feel new shapes respectively, and to find new tying pathways together.

This shibari course is aimed at practitioners who already have suspension experience and are looking to get more creative with these skills. Please be mindful of your own skillset when applying any techniques from this collection to your practice.

title: Positional Study For Futomomo
about:
In this shibari class, Fuoco discusses best practices for labbing futomomos with her model Enna.


Discovering what works for you and your body as a rope bottom and being able to make small but impactful modifications together with your rigger is key to confident and comfortable rope labbing sessions.


This class explores the positional adjustments that models or riggers can make in order to make a tie feel either more easily endurable or – should you want a challenge – more strenuous, focusing specifically on futomomos and creating sustainable single-point inversions in these calf-to-thigh harnesses.


Additionally, Fuoco shares her tips and tricks for how to approach loading the body in the air so as to allow the bottom to acclimate to the harness before dialing up the intensity with a single-point suspension.


This class is intended for intermediate to advanced levels and should only be applied to your practice if you already have some suspension experience. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own practice.

about:
In this step-by-step shibari class, Gorgone teaches various options for closing the rope at the end of a tie with their model De’Jon.

From basic anchoring knots to wrapping rope around the body to finishing up your first tie, everything we do with rope bondage is a combination of basic anchoring knots, wrapping and frictions. This class will show you several easy and effective options for closing your ties to that they stay secure and in in place for play.

After learning the single-column and double-column ties, forward and reverse tension and a few simple closing options, you have enough tools to start playing around with rope in a creative way and explore free tying sensual floor-play. It can be that easy!

title: Tanuki Tsuri
about:
In this class, Gestalta teaches a Tanuki Tsuri ("racoon suspension") with their model Olivia.

Minimalistic and challenging on the body, the focus of this advanced tie is on acrobatic prowess and dynamic movement. The transition from face-up (forward fold) to face-down (backbend) is very impressive and may be an interesting exercise for experienced models who enjoy intense proactive bottoming experiences. It will challenge their proprioception and autonomous body coordination in the rope. If you enjoy playing with ties that test both flexibility and stamina, this one is for you! However, as this tie requires a high level of flexibility and resilience from the bottom, it should not be attempted with inexperienced partners.

As Gestalta explains, this tie is intended to be short-lived and should only be suspended with a pulley in order to lift and lower the body swiftly and smoothly, relieving pressure on the wrists as fast and regularly as needed.

We highly recommend negotiating practicing this strenuous tie very carefully and thoroughly to ensure everyone understands that the risks of injury are higher with this suspension. The main risks associated with this tie are nerve compression on the wrists and back/shoulder injury during the transition from the face-up position into a fairly extreme backbend. This class is aimed at advanced riggers and bottoms alike.

title: Rope as a Language
about:
In this rope bondage series, Anna Bones explores some of the fundamentals for bringing nuance and awareness to your tying practice with her model Nuur.

In the first class, ‘Rope as a Language’, Anna teaches how to simple rope and body handling techniques can make a serious difference in your tying sessions. After all, when it comes to rope bondage, knowing how to tie various knots and frictions is just one part of the practice. Arguably as important is knowing how to handle your rope and understanding how different ways of using speed, tension and tempo can create different sensations and even emotions for your partner, so setting the tone for various types of play. During the course of the class, Anna shares her insights into how rope can be a form of communication.

In the second class, ‘Form and Ropes’, Anna teaches the fundamentals of tying with the contours of your partner’s body. Learning good tying habits early on will put you on an advantageous footing as your bondage practice advances. One such habit is understanding that the idea is not to place your rope in straight lines across the body and starting to observe the shape of the body to guide your rope placement instead.

This class is dedicated helping beginners not only master this important skill but also understand why and how to apply it as they progress, with emphasis on tying the torso and hips. As Anna explains, this is an explorative exercise, akin to drawing on the body with the rope.


While this series is aimed at beginners, we encourage everyone to take some time to brush up on the basics. The foundations of your bondage practice are laid here.

title: Creating Imbalance In Floor Play
about:
In this shibari course, Docvale and Bänana discuss how the intentional use of imbalance in ropes can create an element of surprise and intensity.


You need to have good understanding of how to create and control balance in order to start playing with intentionally disrupting it, says Docvale (check out the ‘Creating Balance’ course as a starting point). While creating balance can refine your communication in ropes, mindfully exploring imbalance can be a playful way to create new physical and psychological challenges, even in floor play.


In the first tutorial, the pair use the example of forearm lacing to begin introducing this type of movement manipulation. This particular harness is a useful tool to begin exploring how the quality of your communication translates to ease of play. As explained by Docvale, you want to invite movement rather than force it in order to better help the person being tied relax into the ropes.


In the second tutorial, a Strappado is used to further demonstrate how creating imbalance can be an effective and highly visceral tool for more psychological rope play. During the class, Docvale offers various options for turning up the intensity by further compressing the body to make maintaining balance even trickier.


Finally, in the third tutorial, Docvale demonstrates how this type of play can be used in a cross-legged ebi position. While this position may seem highly stable, it only takes some compacting and a little manipulating the body to create total imbalance even here.


This course is suitable for all levels, although it’s recommended that you get comfortable with the ‘Creating Balance’ series first, before you begin playing with imbalance.

title: Simple Pyramid Tie
about:
In this step-by-step shibari class, Fred Hatt teaches a basic version of his predicament tie, the Pyramid Tie, with his model Briki.

Predicament ties are Fred’s favourite form of rope play. Endurance, impossible choices, and playing with his bottom’s headspace are the key ingredients in the equation. In this class, Fred teaches a simple form of his Pyramid Tie. This tie is a perfect entry point to predicament play, using only simple knots while conveying clearly the concept of threat versus effort in a tie.

While offering a follow-along explanation of how to tie the Pyramid Tie, Fred also shares detailed explanations about balance, body mechanics and build-up (of ties and endorphins) for both riggers and rope bottoms.

This tie requires a suspension point and is suitable for intermediate levels and beyond. This tie can be difficult to achieve without good knowledge of the body and in this form of play rigger and model are working ‘against’ each other rather than with each other, so it becomes important to recognise ways in which the model can ‘cheat’ while always paying extreme attention to detail and body cues to keep the bottom safe.

title: Kinoko's Forearm Binder
about:
In this class, Hajime Kinoko teaches his Forearm Binder with his model Maya Homerton.

Equal parts bold and intricate, straightforward and complex, when used on its own, this snug structure’s impressive aesthetic belies just how easy it is to tie – in fact, it’s perfect for Shibari beginners. It can also offer an exciting challenge to more practiced students wanting to use it for suspension.

This forearm binder works well for vertical suspensions with most of the load on the lower body and care should be taken not to create too much load on the hands. We recommend using it paired with our Hip Loader (or a hip-loaded variation of the Butterfly Harness) to create stunning and comfortable vertical suspensions that ask nothing more of the bottom’s hands and arms than to look beautiful!

title: Kinoko's Bedroom Bondage
about:
In this shibari tutorial series, Kinoko teaches two harnesses that can be used in the bedroom (and beyond), together with his model hua hua.

Many beginner shibari learners first become interested in rope for its erotic applications, and while advanced suspensions and intense rope scenes may end up having their place in your practice, they’re not exactly bedroom-friendly. In this course, Kinoko teaches his take on shibari for sex with two ties that are straightforward, functional and fun. Importantly, Kinoko emphasizes that these harnesses are designed for comfort, sustainability and, well, the high likelihood of getting distracted during this type of play. As such, they’re easy to tie and untie and can be tied more loosely than some other shibari harnesses.

In the first video, Kinoko teaches an arms-front harness that plays with the feelings of being restrained while also being an easy position for the person being tied to maintain over a longer period.

In the second video, Kinoko offers a hip harness variation built for grabbing, tugging and pulling in all sorts of positions while still being simple to tie and comfortable to be in.

The third video offers pointers for how these harnesses can be used for play, making for bedroom bondage that mitigates the risks of more advanced ties while still being playful, intimate and spicy.

This class is suitable for beginner levels and beyond. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own rope practice. Remember, too, that consent and negotiation are integral to all types of rope play. Before beginning to experiment with these ties, decide in advance how you will use these harnesses, check in regularly during and remember that play can be stopped at any time if either partner feels uncomfortable.

title: Half-Mermaid
about:
In this shibari class, Lief and Icky teach their version of the Half-Mermaid harness, as well as demonstrating how to suspend it.

Binding the legs together from the waist to just above the knees, the Half-Mermaid harness is a great alternative to a booty basket or hip harness: suspendable, supportive and ultra-snug. Lief and Icky’s take on the tie builds in additional lower back support as well as extra cinches to prevent the rope from traveling into the nervy knee pit area. As Lief explains, no band is purely decorative – every rope is placed intentionally and to offer support.

In the first part of the class, they teach the step-by-step Half-Mermaid pattern, detailing important safety tips, including how best to keep the bottom stable as you tie and how to avoid impinging on the nerves and tendons in the back of the knees. They also offer guidelines for how to ensure the correct tension before attempting to suspend the tie.

In the second part of the class, you’ll learn where and how to load the Half-Mermaid tie, and from there, how to suspend it.

This course is great if you’re looking to level up your lower body harnesses and learn some new leg tie variants. However, please keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from these classes and only use this harness in suspension if that is already a part of your rope practice.

title: Predicament Progress
about: Predicaments are ties that create choice…typically a choice between one discomfort or another. The name of the game is time. Riggers: sit back and enjoy the view as your partner explores, sinks into discomfort, and finally starts to sweat. Bottoms: the choice is yours when to tap out. Predicaments ask you to calm your mind, steady your breath, and suffer a little…or a lot. If you’re new to predicaments, these handful of videos will give you some easy exploration opportunities before ramping up to more intense positions. We’ve included a lot of content for folks newer to using suspension lines for play as well as our video on hand checks, as we’ll be working with box tie positions here. Make sure to give that content a refresh if you need it.

title: Suspending Someone Heavier Than Yourself
about:
In this special shibari session, Bänana discusses how she approaches suspending someone heavier than herself with her model Fred.

Tying well often means knowing how to adapt, says Bänana, and tying someone heavier than yourself shouldn’t be viewed as a problem but simply as another parameter to be considered and adjusted for during the tying session.

During this demonstration and discussion, Bänana explains how pulleys, suspension lines, body handling and mechanics can be managed when suspending someone heavier than you. As she shows throughout the class, even small tweaks can add up to easier and more effective suspensions regardless of the whether the person being tied is heavier than the person doing the tying.


This shibari tutorial is suitable for intermediate and advanced students who already have some suspension experience.

about:
In this shibari course, Docvale discusses how the position of the body in ropes can be used as a breath play tool with his model Bänana.


If you’re looking for rope play that will quite literally take your breath away, you’ve come to the right course. As a follow-up to ‘Rope As A Breath Play Tool’, the French instructors continue to delve into breath restriction as an element of rope scenes, focusing on three positions that use compression or alignment of the body to influence the breathing of the person being tied. The classes also explore tips and tricks for playing with intensity in each of these positions, as well as offering feedback from Bänana regarding her experience in the ties.


In the ‘Arch’ video, Docvale uses the example of a floor-based Gyaku Ebi or hog tie to illustrate how an arched position puts pressure on key parts of the respiratory system, while the compression of gravity against the ground and the tie itself prevents the rib cage from fully expanding.


In the ‘Torsion’ video, Docvale uses a semi-suspended ‘mermaid’ position to discuss the role of twisting the body at the waist as a means for influencing the breath with variations for creating more or less pressure.


In the ‘Compacted Position’ video, Docvale offers some ideas for how to use compression and compaction – in this case, starting with a loaded TK as a basis for beginning to wrap the knees towards the chest.


Breath play is a powerful type of edge play, so it’s essential to keep in mind that while elements of this course may be applicable to your own practice, restricting a person’s breath can have a profound physical and psychological impact and is never without risk. It is essential for both you and your tying partner to understand these risks before attempting to recreate anything you see in these classes. If your skill set is not suitable to safely attempt this course, feel free to watch the class for inspiration but do not follow along.

title: Microbondage
about:
In this shibari course, Anoxia delves into the minutia of Microbondage with their model fuoco.

What is this, bondage for ants? No, it’s microbondage, the shibari technique dedicated to tying smaller, delicate structures, such as fingers, toes and faces. As Anoxia explains, there are many reasons to tie on this tiny scale. Whether it’s a greater sense of completion as you get to these final details, creating a stronger sense of immobilization, playing with highly sensitive parts of the body or intentionally amplifying certain emotions in a tie, microbondage is a little guy with an outsized impact. In this class series, you will learn two different microbondage techniques as well as tips for safer, smarter tying.

Safety first! Because microbondage focuses on parts of the body that may be more susceptible to injury if tied improperly, the first part of this course is all about important safety considerations. In this class, Anoxia details the risks of microbondage as well as tips for how to mitigate some of these risks.

In videos that follow, Anoxia teaches two approaches to microbondage: through stretch and through pinning. As well as demonstrating how to do each, they also explain when stretch may be more appropriate and when pinning may be more appropriate. Imperative always? Slowing down and bringing awareness to being extra attentive.

This course is appropriate for anyone who already feels confident tying on the macro level (think harnesses, arm binders, leg ties and floor play) and feels ready to zoom in a little. Bottoms should have good body awareness, and clear communication on both sides of the rope is essential.

about:
In this class Fred Hatt teaches the 'Bones & Ropes' Leg-Tie with his model Mio. This tie was designed together with his partner Anna Bones.

This tie is a more comfortable and versatile alternative to classic futomomos, minus the painful pressure on the shinbone typical of the futomomo and allowing more freedom of movement because the leg can be either bent or kept open.

It can be used in the same fashion for single-point inversions or in combination with a loaded chest harness to create various positions and transitions, as demonstrated in the Suspension video. It is a wonderful tie to use for Self Suspension as it can be tied and attached to the suspension point standing.

The Demo video is a straightforward version of the same tie without talking. It is useful to overview the harness before studying the tutorial or to refresh your memory after you have watched the tutorial with full explanations.

title: Mid-Air Futomomos
about:
In this step-by-step shibari tutorial series, Fuoco explores how to gain confidence tying futomomos in mid-air with her model Enna.


Being able to apply a harness in the middle of a transition scene while your model is suspended is an incredibly useful skill as your rope bondage practice advances. It’s a tool that allows for both longer scenes and better quality of scenes by increasing your options, expanding opportunities for release and relaxation, and – ultimately – helping you develop dynamic tying that will add to the sustainability of your suspension sequences. That is, provided you’re able to do it both well and quickly enough for your model to benefit. However, as you will learn in this two-part futomomo-focused course, tying in the air is very different to tying on the ground and there are numerous variables to consider and account for.


In the first video, Fuoco presents some exercises for tying a futomomo in mid-air with your model in a side suspension. While ungrounded, this is generally a position that doesn’t require a high level of endurance, and gives the option of applying the futomomo to either the top or bottom leg. This class explores how these factors may influence your tying and how to navigate any challenges that arise.


In the second video, you will learn how to practice mid-air futomomos from a more challenging kata-ashi position, which – like the previous drill – comes with its own considerations to manage as you tie.


This class is intended for advanced shibari learners only. These exercises have been developed to help you increase your confidence as you tie in mid-air, so we recommend taking your time to give each drill ample practice and attention. If your skill set is not suitable to safely attempt this course, feel free to watch the class for inspiration but do not follow along.

title: Considerations for Self-Tying
about:
In this shibari course, Anansi shares a series of self-tying primer tutorials designed to help beginners explore the many benefits of self-tying and develop confidence in their practice. Additionally, she offers some ideas for connective exercises for roping others into your self-tying with her models Reemah, Lavender, Enna and Kahrin.

When we think of shibari as a tool for exploring connection and intention, it’s all too easy to forget that not only can these elements be explored without a tying partner but there are real benefits to be derived from tying solo too. This course is built around a series of easy and fun floor-based self-tying exercises that focus on cultivating different facets of self-tying rather than simply recreating certain patterns. As Anansi explains, self-tying can allow practitioners to improve essential rope bottoming skills such as processing various sensations, exploring different types of movement and mindful breathing.

The first two exercises offer starting prompts and intentions to explore both less and more dynamic types of self-tying, so focusing more on stillness or more on movement.

In the next three classes, Anansi demonstrates how self-tying can, in fact, still be a group activity with a series of connective exercises that explore… tying yourself to others!

Finally, the group ties conclude with a casual debrief as the participants discuss what they most enjoyed about these playful takes on connective tying.

This course is suitable for all levels and, with plenty of room for free-styling and adjusting to your own needs, can be adapted for just about any skill set. Remain mindful of your abilities and allow this series to inspire your rope practice accordingly.

title: Handling Drills For Flow
about:
In this shibari course, Fuoco teaches a series of drills together with her model Cat. These tie-along videos are designed for you to return to time and again, any time your rope handling needs to be dusted off.

Learning patterns may be integral to your shibari journey but so is connecting with your partner. If exploring intent and connection tends to take a backseat to perfecting patterns, developing your rope handling skills is an easy way to level up without the need for a lot of new knots and frictions. Getting comfortable with these drills will help you to tie more smoothly, quickly and confidently, so you can give more of your attention to the person in your rope as you wrap them up.

Finger Hooking: In the first drill video, Fuoco discusses finger hooking technique and offers three variations of the same exercise, utilizing finger hooking skills and three different frictions to create a simple mermaid tie. You’re encouraged to follow along however works best for you. Tie along on a chair or table. Adapt the drill to tie your partner’s upper body once you feel comfortable with tying on the legs. Keep it interesting for yourself but just keep coming back!

Make a Stick: This drill video is all about how to pass rope between the body and other ropes with smoothness and ease. Follow along with Fuoco as she does the drill herself in real time. Notice if, with practice, you’re able to keep pace with her and see your rope handling skills improving! If you don’t have a model to practice with, this drill can absolutely be adapted to work on a piece of furniture or your own legs!

Control Your Rope Ends: As we begin to tie faster and with more confidence, rope ends tend to go flying, and these wild rope ends can be a hazard to both you and your bottom. No one likes being popped in the face with a rogue rope end, so learning to control all of your rope – down to your little stopper knots – is important. Join Fuoco as she guides you through a drill designed to help you gain better control of the whole length of your rope.

Laying Your Rope: A drill that can be practiced with a partner or on your own body, this exercise is designed to help you confidently lay rope on a body with even tension, and without twists or gaps. Follow along with Fuoco and Cat and practice laying your rope down well without needing to look at your every move, so that you can give more of your attention to your partner!

This class is suitable for all levels. Even very experienced riggers know the benefit of returning to basic handling drills from time to time. If you’re a total newbie, you might want to familiarize yourself with single column ties and basic frictions first. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own rope practice.

title: Cocoon Tie
about:
In this class, Gorgone teaches the Cocoon Tie with their model Alma.

This surprising tie is very different from the usually highly engineered harnesses presented by Gorgone, offering beautiful old-school aesthetics and a very restrictive feeling. It can be used for floor play or suspension, and will be particularly appealing to those who enjoy playing with exposure and helplessness.

This tie can be easily modified to suit different bodies or aesthetics, however it can be quite unpredictable in the air and shouldn't be suspended without special attention and care for the possibility of nerve compression or slippage of the wraps over the shoulders.

We recommend experimenting with it in partial suspensions before attempting to suspend fully. You can also use a pulley to lift the whole body at once instead of going up by increments as demonstrated in the class.

title: Intentional Third Rope
about:
In this shibari course, hua hua teaches a series of Intentional Third Ropes for TKs with her models Dantianshi and Kahrin.

Why use a third rope in your TKs? As hua hua explains in the first part of this multi-class series, third ropes in shibari are a versatile and often valuable addition to your TK pattern, with various options to explore based on the type of sensation, function or play you want to add to your tie. In other words, determine your needs and intentions and you’ll likely be able to add a third rope approach to match. Applicable to both stemmed and stemless TKs, third ropes can reinforce or add stability to the structure in suspensions, can offer a deeper sense of restriction, or can be included for aesthetic reasons. After diving into the reasons why you might want (or need) to add a third rope, hua hua goes deeper into the how with three examples that you can add to your own favorite TKs, detailing how to tie them as well as the advantages of each.

In the Tasuki class, hua hua teaches a third rope pattern that places rope just inside of and over the shoulders for a chest-opening effect. Demonstrated on both a stemless TK and a stemmed TK, she shares insights into how the Tasuki pattern can offer functional support in stemmed versions, or alternatively, create more of a decorative element in stemless TKs. hua hua also offers tips on how to make it either more or less challenging for the bottom, depending – of course – on your intention.

In the X-shape class, hua hua teaches two versions of a third rope pattern that creates a cross-shape over the chest: one for stemless TKs and one for stemmed TKs. Much like the Tasuki, the X-shape can serve an aesthetic and a functional purpose but, due to the wraps that pass very close to the neck, has some important risk considerations too. An effective tool for amping up sensations of compression and choking, this pattern is best utilized with prior consideration and only when you’ve agreed that you intentionally want to incorporate breath play elements into your tying.

In the V-shape class, hua hua shares both a stemmed and stemless version of her favorite third rope pattern. Constructed to create a V-shape and stem at the front of the harness, this variation creates another supportive structure with which to play – whether that’s breath play, using it to help create more lift in a face-up suspension or for attaching to another part of the body depends entirely on your scene and your intentions.

This course is ideal for riggers who are starting to feel comfortable with tying harnesses and want to bring more intentionality into that area of their practice. While these third rope examples can add important structural support during suspensions, please keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from these classes and only use these harnesses in suspension if that is already a part of your rope practice. Bottoms should be comfortable maintaining a box-tie/TK position.

title: Booty Basket
about:
GO TO BOOTY BASKET HARNESS GUIDE

In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky teach their take on a traditional Booty Basket tie.

An interesting alternative to a gun slinger or hip harness, the booty basket is unique in being a structure that both supports the hips and creates actual restriction. The forced fold of the body at the hips creates very different shapes than traditional hip harnesses. As Lief and Icky explain, they struggled with traditional ways of tying it not offering enough structure and being difficult to tension, so this pattern may be a little different to how you’ve seen it tied before.

In this course, Lief and Icky offer a step-by-step class on how to tie their Booty Basket, for a lower body harness that’s fun on the floor as well as versatile and secure in suspensions. They also teach three different ways of loading the harness for partial suspensions and suspension: from the back, from the side and from the center.

This harness can be utilized in all types of play. However, please keep your skill set in mind and only use it in suspensions if you already have plenty of experience.

title: Study On Falling
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Gorgone will be teaching their ‘Study on Falling’ suspension sequence with their model Vivian.

One of Gorgone’s favorite suspension sequences, they have performed it extensively over the years and now, for the first time ever, will be teaching it on Shibari Study.

Gorgone designed this sequence as a way to surrender to the experience of extreme vulnerability, letting go and “falling” into the rope. As they explain in the class intro, while this may not be too complicated to tie for the rigger, it is a very intense sequence for the person being tied and carries a higher risk profile due to the last position in particular – a single-point waist rope suspension dropping into a fairly extreme backbend shape. As such, it’s essential to go through it slowly, with confidence and with no resistance in the body of the person being tied.


As a suspension sequence that is both physically demanding and at-times psychologically challenging, the class offers insights into ways in which to make it more manageable for the person being tied, such as starting out with a hands-free chest harness to allow the model more control, as well as Gorgone’s tips for how to reassure yourself and your tying partner as you move through this exquisite and powerful progression. They also offer essential advice for warming up beforehand and getting accustomed to the sensation of dropping into the single waist line.


This class is aimed at advanced students with plenty of suspension experience only. Please watch the videos in full, familiarize yourself with the sequence and do not push yourself if you feel any uncertainty or resistance, particularly going into the last position.

title: Handling Drills For Uplines
about:
In this shibari tutorial series, Fuoco shares a number of follow-along drills for uplines, with exercises designed to help you get your uplines up and down as easily and efficiently as possible.

Confident upline management and control is key to safer suspensions in rope. These handling drills are designed to help you practice and perfect tying smoothly and securely, with or without a partner. Tie along, repeat often and practice regularly, and watch your rope handling transform.

The first drill focuses on smart tying techniques for tying and untying an upline that’s locked with two half-hitches (also known as a clove hitch).

The second drill focuses on tying and untying uplines locked with a slipped overhand knot (also known as a Naka bow).

title: Floor Play Flow
about:
In this shibari tutorial course, hua hua teaches a series of rope flows together with her model Dantianshi, specifically curated for enjoying all the various sensations and emotions of tying on the floor.

You don’t need complex ties or advanced techniques to create rope scenes filled with intentionality, engagement and emotion. In fact, you don’t even need to move your scenes beyond the floor. In this multi-part course, hua hua explores a variety of floor-based flows and partial suspensions with a focus on making your ropes intentional, maintaining a strong line of communication between both tying partners, and discovering a spectrum of sensations and emotions. Each tie is designed with plenty of room for adaptation and with different intents and styles – some focused on suffering and endurance, others more on eroticism and connection – to better suit various moods, desires and even rope dynamics.

In the Beast Tie sequence, hua hua and Dantianshi demonstrate a simple-yet-sensual floor-based tie that invites a slower pace and softer interactions. The first video focuses on setting the tone for the tie with advice for how to create a more connective or erotic scene. The second part of this class uses a suspension point to gently elevate then hands and feet, allowing for more vulnerability and different options for play.

The Armbinder flow is a sequence with more direct erotic intent. As hua hua explains, deliberate movements and purposeful physical contact are utilized in this tie to convey forcefulness and heighten anticipation and a sense of vulnerability for the person being tied. Take your time too: the gradual pace of this sensual sequence allows plenty of space to build tension and gauge reactions, so giving the person in ropes room to react and choose if they wish to continue or not. hua hua also offers valuable insights for how to build upon this arm binder and create an even more erotically charged rope scene.

In the Shrimp Tie sequence, hua hua explores a classic shibari shape specifically intended to be more strenuous for the person being tied, particularly on the lower back and hips. Beginning with a detailed explanation of how to build the tie using a minimalist TK and an agura, hua hua offers her tips and tricks to make things more or less challenging and ensure that the only stress points in the tie are intentional. Once the tie is constructed, it’s time to play – as hua hua says during this demo sequence, don’t be tempted to start adding things or changing positions immediately but rather sit and observe. It’s a tie that allows you to play with multiple states of mind, sensations and even types of suffering without changing any rope, so give those feelings time to develop and build up for slower, more deliberate semenawa sessions.

This class is suitable, in part, for beginners. However, we recommend some prior experience with uplines before attempting to recreate the partial suspensions in some of these ties. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own rope practice. As hua hua explains, remember to take time to negotiate and discuss what style and intention is suitable for your dynamic. Before beginning to experiment with these ties, decide in advance how you will use them, check in regularly during and remember that play can be stopped at any time if either partner feels uncomfortable.

title: Beyond Circus
about:
In this course, Fred Hatt teaches two harnesses and a suspension class putting them into use with his model Briki.

Dynamic suspension transitions are often associated with ‘circus bondage’ and stage performances, but for Fred this flavour of rope is also a vehicle for ordeal-based play. In this class, he presents his personal approach to playing with suspension transitions that goes beyond simply creating shapes in the air.


The class has a strong focus on the tempo of this kind of scene which is punctuated by a series of peaks (stress positions) and valleys (or ‘pit-stops) of endorphins and adrenaline, distinct from the tempo of semenawa or torment based play, which focuses more on a gradual crescendo towards the apex of a tie.


When doing dynamic suspensions, Fred likes to feed off his partner's impulses, presenting him with choices to provide relief (or ‘pit stops’) for them, or block movement to cause stress. This offers a contrasted experience and rush to the model, always alternating between challenging positions and moments of rest.


He explains how to read the model’s body and make decisions accordingly, the differences between what he calls ‘micro’ and ‘macro’ transitions, blocking movement versus giving room, playing with endorphins and adrenaline.


We recommend learning and practicing the harnesses taught in separate videos prior to watching the full sequence. The harnesses alone are suitable for intermediate level, however the transition class is geared towards advanced-expert level practitioners.


Note that Fred is using a TK in the classes, but you can replace it with a hands-free harness to reduce the risks of nerve damage and stress in the shoulders.

During the class, Tifereth discusses how to control for the pitch of the harness and the different ways to manage your partner’s body in space as you play with this tie; slowly through line management or, if you’re looking to inject more energy into a scene, quickly through hands-on transitions. She also offers valuable tips for where to find stability as well as how to intensify or offload shapes as you play.

This shibari tutorial is for advanced tying partners who are confident in suspensions, particularly as the Tenshi is designed for bottoms who want more mobility in the air. Remember, this is a progressive practice – start slowly and pick up the pace as you become more proficient. title: Feelings Game
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky share one of their labbing-for-better-rope games to help you and your tying partners build better communication when tying: the Feelings Game.

The Feelings Game is an adaption of an exercise developed by the Devil Mask Society as part of their tying Cell curriculum. That curriculum is open source and can be found on their website: devilmasksociety.com

In shibari, we often speak of rope as a ‘language’ for communicating intent, so how do you make sure nothing gets lost in translation? As Lief and Icky explain, conveying and receiving feeling are the two halves of intent-driven, rewarding rope scenes, and building an effective communication practice and style will better help you feel, well, the things you want to feel. The Feelings Game is a fun and exploratory exercise in building a rope language together with your partner, combining pre-scene negotiation, non-verbal communication skills during tying and, of course, working to convey the desired emotion as clearly as possible.

This class is divided into three parts: a pre-scene negotiation where Icky expresses three feelings they would be open to feeling in ropes during the scene, the non-verbal tying session in which Lief picks one of the negotiated emotions to try to convey, and a debrief interview where we find out of Icky can guess which emotion Lief chose based on their tying alone.

This exercise is suitable for all levels, as long as you allow your own skill set to guide you. Effective communication in ropes doesn’t require complicated techniques or advanced skills – the more you play this game, the more you will come to learn just that!

Not sure what you want to feel in ropes today? Check out this list for some emotional inspiration.

title: Strappado | Armbinders
about:
In this class, Tamandua teaches two variations of strappado (behind-the-back armbinders).

The first variation is easily adaptable for bottoms who may not easily be able to get their elbows close together, while still creating an arm binder that is compact and restrictive. Because this variation of the tie does not support the chest, it’s best utilized for floor-play or partial suspensions only. The second variation with additional wrapping around the chest is suitable for suspensions.

For the suspension line, we recommend using an epsilon on the top wrap for more chest load and eventually add a secondary rope from the wrists to lift the arms. For partial suspensions, you may also attach a rope directly from the wrists with an epsilon for a more extreme variation, as demonstrated in the free Strappado Session demo.

Strappado ties are fairly demanding on the body and involve a higher risk of nerve compression and blood circulation issues – we recommend doing regular hand checks and practicing these ties with extra care.
