title: First Flight: Side Suspension
about:
This playlist is part of our Rope Resolutions challenge to help make 2026 your knottiest year yet, so practice regularly this January to earn your streaks and win a prize. Find all of the details in our Community!

Pre-requisites: An upper body harness that is suitable for side suspensions. The rigger should know it by memory, and it should be comfortable and sustainable for the bottom. Choose a harness that you've tied together several times and test loaded at least once. We’ve included the Misungui harness here, but you’re welcome to use any upper body harness that can be side-loaded.

This playlist is specially curated for riggers and bottoms who are ready to start exploring suspension – in other words, those who have already been learning suspendable harnesses, practicing tying uplines with inanimate objects, and practicing clear communication in floorwork and partials. From safety to skills and drills, this collection will help you do the groundwork to get your shibari practice airborne.

We curated this playlist for you to return to and learn from slowly and gradually. Make time to learn the information but also to develop habits around practicing rope regularly. If the harnesses are unfamiliar, drill them and lab them till they go on with great tension and flow. If uplines aren’t in your muscle memory, don’t move on until you feel more confident. The final video is there for you when you both feel excited, not nervous, about the challenge.

Heads up: Please take these considerations in mind before attempting the final class:
· We strongly recommend you do your first suspensions with the supervision of a trusted instructor.
· If attempting this at home, have a spotter or second person available to assist in the instance that you need to come down quickly.
· Gorgone uses a combination of lock-off techniques. There are many right ways to finish an upline, and it’s not necessary that you recreate exactly what is shown in the video, though we strongly recommend using the double U-lock where indicated.
· If this is your first time working through this course, avoid joining your uplines as you see in the video. That technique should only be added after you feel confident in your ability to sustain this position for some time, as joining lines increases the amount of time needed to come down from suspension.
· If the final position is uncomfortable, consider bringing the ankle to the point as well.

Building on the elements of using both your rope and your body for pushing, pulling and stretching as taught in Tifereth’s ‘Physical Rope: Ground’ class, the second part of this series adds an extra dynamic to your physical rope toolbox: gravity.

The first drill, ‘Playing With Gravity’, is designed to help you find flow and movement in a partial suspension starting out with some simple wrist cuffs. As Tifereth explains, you should stick to this drill for as long as you need to get a feel for this dynamic and connective way of tying. For the person being tied, this is also an opportunity to practice active participation, communication and awareness of how you hold yourself in these types of ties.

The second drill, ‘Making Connections’, expands on the skills you practiced in the first, adding more rope and getting deeper into this style of rope with Tifereth demonstrating where you might find opportunities as well as how to playfully exploit them. Be prepared to feel awkward at first, she says. The rope is simple – wraps and single-columns – but the technique is what comes with time and practice. The more you practice the deeper mechanics of body manipulation play, the more confident you’ll become. For Tifereth and Irkalla, this hands-on type of tying is one of their favorite ways to connect, allowing their dynamic to shine.

This class requires some experience with partial suspensions and tying suspension lines. To explore play with these techniques for any level of experience, check out the Physical Rope: Ground’ class.

In this insightful shibari and anatomy tutorial series, Reemah discusses how the same types of ties can be adapted for different bodies with her models Anansi and Lavender.


Rope is not a one-size-fits-all practice. What works for one person’s body may be totally unsustainable or incorrectly placed on the next. In this essential course, Reemah offers useful guidelines for how to use the anatomy of the person being tied to determine your rope placement for various parts of the body, so making for more sturdy, sustainable and safer ties.


In the first video, Reemah advises on how to approach arms-front harnesses and how different chest sizes require adaptations in your placement.


In the second video, she discusses the rope placement of harness that bring the arms behind the back, such as the TK.


In the third video, Reemah demonstrates the same technique to find the waist for a waist rope on her two different models – resulting in two seemingly vastly different placements. As she emphasizes throughout the series, this is a function of adjusting your rope for the person being tied.


Finally, in the fourth video, Reemah explores thigh cuffs and the various anatomical factors that can help you tie better cuffs on any body you encounter.


This shibari tutorial series is appropriate and recommended for all levels. Better bondage begins with understanding that rope is a tool that can be adapted to any body, not the other way around.

title: Minimalistic Waist Tie
about:
In this step-by-step shibari class, Gorgone teaches an easy and minimalistic Belly Hug waist tie with their mode Aleks.

With just one or two ropes and a very simple structure, this straightforward tie with the arms crossed over the belly still manages to feel constrictive and efficiently locks the arms in place. This quick but efficient tie is suitable for all levels and perfect for floor sessions. Best of all, it can be creatively reimagined or added to as your shibari skills develop, making it one you’re sure to keep coming back to.

This tie is suitable for most bodies and can be easily adapted to the flexibility and preferences of the person being tied, making it ideal for beginner floor play sessions using just one or two ropes.

title: Tengu Harness
about:
GO TO TAM’S TENGU HARNESS GUIDE

In this class, Tamandua teaches his variation of the Tengu with his model Mie Neko.

The Tengu (or “demon” tie) is a versatile modern Shibari harness, the position of which is inspired by the wings of the Tengu, mythological creatures featuring large wings.

Though the chest-opening position created by the Tengu accentuates vulnerability and exposure of the front body, it is, in fact, a very stable and sustainable tie that doesn’t require too much flexibility from the model and is suitable for all body types.

This harness is also perfectly suspendable, meaning that it can be utilized as an alternative to a TK, if they are not suited to your partner or if you'd like to try a different shape. This harness can be loaded from the front or back as demonstrated in the suspension video.

The harness alone is a suitable tie for intermediate level riggers, though using it for suspension is only advised for advanced practitioners. Tamandua also demonstrates another version of the Tengu for floor-play using bamboo in his series 'Semenawa Bamboo Ties'.

title: Self-Suspension Uplines And The Body
about:
In this self-tying shibari class, Kissmedeadlydoll explores Self-Suspension Uplines and the Body with her model… herself! In this course, you’ll learn how both uplines and your own body can be important tools for a creative and dynamic self-suspension practice.

After more than a decade of self-tying and self-suspending, Kissmedeadlydoll has learnt a thing or two about how to do-it-yourself in ropes. From active bottoming through new shapes, creative transitions into inversions, and even a nifty trick that’ll turn a removable thigh cuff into a new hard point, this course is all about making your uplines and your body work for you in self-suspensions.

This self-suspension course is divided into five parts, beginning with an introduction and lecture, before moving on to three classes that demonstrate different skills and options available to self-tyers in practice. Finally, Kissmedeadlydoll combines all the skills demonstrated in the previous videos to show how torsions, rotations, transitions from face-up to face-down, and more can be accessible to self-suspenders with clever upline and body involvement.

This course is aimed at self-tyers who already have some suspension experience. As Kissmedeadlydoll explains, spend some time planning your suspensions, deciding where you want to go and mapping out your journey to get there. Allow this course to inspire and guide you as far as your skill set will allow.

title: Agura & Ebi
about:
In this class, Gorgone teaches a floor-based Agura & Ebi Shibari with her model Jewelryandfire.

Modern Shibari refers to any crossed-leg sitting position as Agura Shibari. If the upper body is tied and forced close to the open legs, it is called Ebi Shibari (shrimp tie) or Ebi Seme (shrimp torment). The body being bent forward and the knees widely spread, the position resembles the body and tail of a prawn or shrimp.

This classic Shibari is inspired by an ancient method of torture, ebi-zeme (海老責め). If kept for a long period of time, this position will heavily restrict the breathing and generate strong blood flow restrictions creating a burning sensation throughout the entire body.

The modern adaptations of this tie offer safer and less tortuous options, for example by replacing the TK with a less restrictive chest-harness and adapting the severity of the forward bend to your partner's ability and preference. You can play around with different levels of intensity by using either a hands-free harness (easier) or a Strappado (harder).

title: Understanding Rope For Bottoms Who Don’t Tie
about:
In this series of rope bondage classes, Fuoco, together with her model Enna, discusses why it’s highly beneficial for bottoms to have a good grasp of how rope works and how being tied should and shouldn’t feel.


Understanding how rope works is an incredibly useful bottoming skill that's rarely taught for the purpose of better bottoming. Understanding the basics of how rope works can help empower bottoms to independently assess the skill level of riggers they'd like to tie with and make collaborative decisions about what sort of rope to do together. Additionally, it can make for more constructive feedback and even collaborative problem-solving when things aren't working, allowing the person being tied to better understand where an issue may be arising rather than seeing themselves or their body as the problem.


In the first class in the course, Fuoco explores tension in ropes, demonstrating how a harness with good tension should look and feel versus one with poor tension.


The second class focuses on frictions with Fuoco providing important information about the specific purpose of frictions within a tie as well as demonstrating examples of how to visually assess whether or not a friction is doing its job.


The third video of this series looks at balance in terms of both symmetry and the ability of a tie to distribute load evenly. In this class, Fuoco offers valuable advice for both how to see and feel if a tie is imbalanced.


Finally, in the fourth class, Fuoco discusses how visually assessing up-lines can be an essential tool to help assess a potential rigger’s suspension readiness or their confidence in suspensions, with tips for easy-to-check features of suspension lines.


The goal of this series is to help bottoms, especially those who don't tie or are new to rope, determine what sort of rope they feel comfortable engaging in with a new-to-them partner. As such, this course is suitable for beginners and may also be helpful for riggers who are just starting out too. We encourage you to always keep your skillset in mind and always adopt a ‘low and slow’ approach if you are new to shibari.

title: Kinoko’s Fuse Ebi Tie
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Kinoko teaches his Fuse Ebi Tie (‘face-down shrimp’ tie) with his model hua hua.

As Kinoko explains, one of the challenges shibari students often encounter in the jump from learning harnesses on the floor to learning how to suspend them is how to maintain balance between left and right. Using Kinoko’s Updated TK3 as a starting point, begin to perfect finding balance in your ties with this floor-based hogtie that uses the body against itself to create some of the same challenges that bottoms will encounter in suspensions. The Fuse Ebi is a tie that demands an equal shape and precise uniform tension on both sides, plus being floor-based, is more sustainable for the person being tied – in short, the perfect tie to practice creating balance before moving on to suspensions. And with its exposing spread-legged position and sustainability making it ideal for foreplay or abandonment play, you might just be able to think of a few other applications for it too…

This class is suitable for intermediate levels and beyond. Always remember to keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from any Shibari Study class to your own rope practice.

title: Improvised Suspension Session With hua hua And Dantianshi
about:
From this mesmerizing shibari performance, long-term tying partners hua hua and Dantianshi share an improvised and intuition-led suspension session as well as a post-rope feedback session.

Sometimes slow and deliberate and at others quicker and more intense, making space for spontaneity while finding familiar touchpoints inform this off-the-cuff seme-inspired performance by hua hua and Dantianshi. Playing with pacing, distance, and different levels – both literally in full and partial suspensions and in terms of intensity – the pair demonstrate an unrehearsed and fully improvised advanced suspension sequence. As they explain in the feedback interview that follows, embracing a lack of structure when tying feels like their most authentic way to connect in ropes. Each tie is not only a reflection of their state of mind but a chance to get to know each other again.

This performance is not an instructional video but is suitable for anyone to watch and enjoy. Please do not attempt recreate anything you see here unless you are at the appropriate skill level and well-practiced in the techniques involved.

title: Frictions Lexicon
about:
This shibari course by Gorgone teaches the fundamental frictions used in rope bondage with her model Miah.

These shibari frictions have various functionalities, from changing direction, to creating stems and solid wraps, to isolating various tensions throughout a tie. They are building blocks used to reinforce, connect or isolate the simple wrappings you've learned in the previous classes and combine them into more sophisticated patterns.

  • Half Hitch

  • Munter Hitch

  • X Friction

  • Half-Moon

  • L Friction

  • Hojo Cuffs

  • Mix it up!

Shibari is like rope Lego! Once you have learned and mastered the basic shibari knots, the shibari wrappings and these fundamental frictions, you can combine them to recreate existing patterns or use your imagination to create endless variations and new combinations. You will start noticing that anything you tie, from the most simple to the most intricate pattern, is always a combination of the same simple elements.

Find inspiring ways to use your new skills in the following courses;
Simple Self-Ties, Simple Harnesses, Minimalistic Ties, Less is More.

title: TK Lab
about:
In this class, Fred Hatt explains and deconstructs the principle functions of the two main families of TK with his model Mio.

What is a Takate Kote (TK)? How does it work and what makes it work? Stem or stemless TK: how are they different? What is ‘high hands’ anyway?

In this class, Fred will share some of his insights regarding key aspects of TK mechanics by demonstrating how TK’s vary in their construction across various families.  The aim of the class is to help consolidate knowledge and demonstrate how every choice you make in rope is, as in life, a compromise.  

 By the end of the class, you should realise that every decision in rope is a compromise, and that the existing TK patterns are complete systems designed for the people and the contexts in which they are typically used. 

This is a very important class for students who struggle with finding the right TK and need to deepen their understanding of the different types of logic and engineering available to them.

title: Suspension Points 101 (FREE)
about:
In this free shibari course, Fred Hatt teaches how to set up a Suspension Point. Learn various methods to create hanging points using props like a sling, a pulley, bamboo, or a carabiner. We recommend watching these videos in the order they are presented here.


The first 'Intro' video is a short introduction covering some safety considerations and an overview of the different options available.


In the video 'Comparing Suspension Points', Fred goes over the differences between using a ring, a bamboo or carabiners for your suspensions. He explains some of the advantages and limitations of each option.


In the video 'Setting Up A Sling', he explains and demonstrates different ways of using a climbing sling to set up a ring or carabiners from a hard point.


In the video 'Setting Up A Bamboo', he explains and demonstrates how to tie off and set up a bamboo for suspensions. Please note that this method requires two separate hard points and should never be installed from a single hard point with both lines coming together in a triangle shape.


In the video 'Using Carabiners', he explains which types of carabiners are safe to use and demonstrates with his model Mio how to use them properly for your uplines. Using carabiners is very different to using a ring or a bamboo because the lines tend to jam and get stuck if not executed properly.


In the video 'Setting Up A Pulley', he teaches how to create a pulley system using a rope and carabiners. This technique is particularly useful for very intense suspensions meant to be short-lived, if you are new to suspensions and want to have an easy way out, or to smoothen out the lifts and drop-downs if your partner is significantly heavier than you.


Please make sure that the hard point(s) you are using when setting up a suspension point is safe and has been installed by a professional or has been tested prior to suspending yourself or a partner.

title: First Flight Futomomo
about:
GO TO FIRST FLIGHT FUTOMOMO HARNESS GUIDE

In this shibari tutorial, Fuoco teaches the First Flight Futomomo with her model Enna.

“The perfect futomomo doesn’t exi—” Okay, okay, maybe the perfect futomomo doesn’t exist, but as you’ll see, the First Flight Futomomo checks plenty of boxes. As Fuoco explains, it’s an especially good option if you’re looking for a variation to begin trying to tie during suspensions. While more rope may make a futumomo more robust and comfortable, less makes it easier to tie in the air: this one happily meets somewhere in the middle, being built for both supportiveness and ease of getting on swiftly.

During the class, Fuoco offers options for how to start, based on your own preference, and step-by-step instructions for how to build the tie, as well as tensioning tips for maximum sustainability.

This course is great for anyone looking for a go-to futomomo for play in the air or on the ground. However, please keep your skill set in mind when applying techniques from this class and only use this harness in suspension if that is already a part of your rope practice.

title: First Flight: Face Up
about:
This playlist is part of our Rope Resolutions challenge to help make 2026 your knottiest year yet, so practice regularly this January to earn your streaks and win a prize. Find all of the details in our Community!

Pre-requisites: An upper body harness that is suitable for face-up suspensions. The rigger should know it by memory, and it should be comfortable and sustainable for the bottom. Choose a harness that you’ve tied together several times and test loaded at least once or simply use the harness suggested in this playlist.

This playlist is designed for riggers and bottoms in the early days of their suspension practice when support, stability and sustainability matter most. If you’ve already been learning suspendable harnesses, using inanimate objects to develop upline skills, and can confidently communicate with your tying partner on the floor and in partials, this one is for you. This collection is all about guiding you towards that first face-up suspension – think safety, drills and skills, and the perfect hands-front harness for achieving lift-off.

While there’s room for adaptation, the simplest way to learn this is to use the suggested harnesses. If you want to use a separate hip harness and other upper body harness, that could work too. You could give yourself an added challenge of opting for a different upper body harness but using the same logic as in the video to incorporate hip support. Consider: how does the hip support get added and what elements would you need to see/not see to know if you could do the same thing to a different upper body harness?

Our suspension playlists are made for slow and gradual learning. Give yourself plenty of time to learn the information and to practice as you go. Only once you feel confident with one technique is it time to move onto the next. By the time you reach the final video, all the skills and techniques you use should feel like muscle memory and like you’re well prepared for the exciting challenge ahead.

Heads up: For your safety, read through the following considerations before attempting the final class:
· If possible, always do your first suspensions under the in-person supervision of a trusted instructor.
· If attempting this outside of a rope studio environment, have another person available to assist in case of an emergency.
· There’s an important "double bight" technique contained within the basic anchoring course. Make sure you find it and understand it so you can use it in the final suspension.

title: Torsions On A Ring
about:
In this class, Gorgone teaches two basic torsion suspensions on a ring with her model Mickael. Torsions can be quite challenging, especially when tied on a ring instead of a bamboo and if not executed smoothly and progressively on both sides of the rope.

In the first class, Gorgone teaches a basic 'S' suspension and explains the importance of uplines levels with the more severe angles created by a ring and how the model can actively participate in creating a smooth lift into the air. In the second video, she demonstrates a low suspension using the Basket Tie and her TK2 for a more gentle torsion.

Feel free to replace the TK with any other tie that suits your partner's needs better if needed.

title: Maximalism Session With Docvale And Bänana (FREE)
about:
In this powerful shibari inspiration session from Docvale and Bänana, the French rope educators flip their previous Minimalism Session on its head, instead exploring how using plenty of rope on the body can create diverse physical and psychological states.

‌

In their years of practicing ropes together, Docvale and Bänana have often taken a ‘less is more’ approach to tying. However, in this intense scene, they explore ‘more is more’ with a focus on full-body lacing combined with a strappado. The resulting suspension sequence spans a physical and emotional spectrum ranging from supportive and comfortably cocooned to strenuous and oppressive and back again.

about:
In this step-by-step shibari course, Fred Hatt teaches two leg ties with his model Briki. These leg harnesses are suitable for all types of play, ranging from on the floor to incorporated into dynamic suspension transitions.

In the first class, Fred teaches a side-loading hip harness (also known as a ‘Gun Slinger’). This harness is typically used for side suspensions but can also support various positions in dynamic transition sequences. It can also be used for self-suspension.

In this class, Fred Hatt teaches a very fast futomomo, a type of leg tie that secures the calf and ankle to the thigh. The clever engineering of this tie makes it incredibly easy and quick to tie, which is important if you want to tie a futo while your model is already in the air. With some practice this tie can be executed in a couple of minutes and is perfectly safe for suspensions.

title: Floor to Air Challenge: The Raven
about:
This playlist is part of our Floor to Air Challenge. Find all of the details in our Community!

Quick, dirty, and anything but simple. Using only a basic chest harness and a double column tie, it’s no surprise that The Raven tie requires some real bottoming skills…and an affinity for a specific flavor of suffering. If you haven’t done much bottoming to rope that smacks you in the face with difficulty and eases off as quickly as it came on, this could be a fun exploration. For the riggers out there, the minimalism of this tie doesn’t let you off the hook. Make sure your double-column tie is on its best behavior! If you’ve never played with a pulley before, this is a fun place to start.

You can swap in any arms free chest harness you like, though be mindful that the verticality of the final position will load the lower wraps, so pay attention to how waist ropes/lower wraps that sit near the sternum affect your experience in the tie. Give it a try, post a pic, and let us know in Community how you liked it!

title: Hojo Cuff Deep Dive
about:
In this shibari course, Fuoco takes a deep dive into the Hojo Cuff with her model Cat.

Hojo cuffs are simply inline single-column ties held together with tension that runs in and tension that runs out, and they can be an incredibly versatile tool to help us avoid unnecessary over-construction of ties. However, to use them effectively, we have to understand how they work and what elements are needed to create bondage that is stable, snug and sustainable. As Fuoco explains, she loves using hojo cuffs for drills and as a learning tool because of what they can teach us about how bodies move and where we can find opportunities to let the fiddly parts of patterns fall away. And whether you’re just learning the ins and outs of hojo cuffs or looking to level up when and how you use them, this course offers something for everybody.

In the first video, you’ll learn what a hojo cuff is with a basic example demonstrating what to keep in mind when tying them and where you might slip up while you’re still getting the hang of them.

In the second video, Fuoco explains the concept of internal tension in the body and how this can be utilized to create more effective and robust hojo cuffs.

The final two videos offer first a lower body challenge and then an upper body challenge. Once you have a confident grasp on the techniques and concepts taught in the first half of the course, these freeform exercises will help you get more creative with your hojo cuff application and realize the (almost) endless possibilities that they offer.

title: Reverse Tension
about:
In this step-by-step shibari class, Gorgone teaches the principle of reverse tension or counter tension with their model De’Jon.

Once you’ve mastered your basic anchoring knots to attach rope to the body, namely the Single-Column Tie and the Double-Column Tie, what to do with the rest of the rope? Everything we do with rope bondage is a combination of basic anchoring knots, wrapping and frictions. This class will introduce you to one of the fundamentals of rope bondage and one of the different ways you can wrap rope around the body – reverse tension. Unlike forward tension, reverse tension adds an extra layer of friction to keep your ropes in place and start building more intricate patterns.

After learning the single-column and double-column ties, forward and reverse tension and a few simple closing options, you have enough tools to start playing around with rope in a creative way and explore free tying sensual floor-play. It can be that easy!

title: Hishi TK
about:
In this class, Gestalta teaches two variations of the Hishi ('diamond') TK with their model Muriel.

The first version is a chest harness only, ending around the waist. The second version goes all the way down through the legs, with the option to separate the wraps around the inner thighs or to keep them running over the crotch.

This pattern follows a different logic than the one used by Kinoko or Gorgone in their diamond-shaped harnesses. Here, the diamonds are created by tying knots along the stem and then pulling them apart instead of building the diamonds in progressive steps with half-hitches and nodomes.

These harnesses are very aesthetically pleasing, but also offer some interesting features for more playful sessions. The pressure points on the front body and increasing tightness as the tie is built make it a perfect structure for Semenawa. It can be used for suspensions or to add a layer of complexity and sensations to your floor-play.

The same anchoring methods can be applied to the full-body version, bearing in mind that the crotch wrap might become tighter according to the position. Make sure to make any adjustments, if necessary.

The full-body variation could be an interesting harness to use on a Hashira (vertical beam) or for a more intense floor-based hog tie, for example!

title: First Harness: Prayer Tie
about:
Experience prerequisites: Nothing but a willingness to learn and level up your shibari skills. Let’s go!

In this beginner-friendly playlist, you’ll be guided through all the skills needed to tie one of your first rope harnesses: the Prayer Hands Harness. Requiring just a few basic knots and frictions as well as some simple techniques, this is the ideal place to start honing and applying your new shibari know-how.

Work through videos in order, moving on to a new technique only once you feel confident in the previous technique. Remember that even simple skills take time to develop, and you'll need both understanding and muscle memory for each component to feel successful when tying the harness. Learn and “lab” the harness before playing with it.

Heads up: Learning can be slow going, so let your tying partners test the position first without rope to make sure it's comfortable enough for them to be tied there for a sustained time.

In this rope bondage tutorial, Anna Bones teaches the Bones & Rope Hip Harness with her model Nuur.

This versatile hip harness is constructed in two parts with the option to stick to a more basic, minimalistic version or to add a third rope for extra structure and support.

Anna developed this tie together with her husband and rope partner Fred Hatt, and says it’s been a go-to for many years as a comfortable and supportive hip harness suitable for dynamic suspensions and self-suspension.

During the course of the class, Anne also shares several tips and tricks for attaching a suspension line, for a hip harness that’s just about as adaptable to your individual needs as they get.

title: Kinoko's Hip Harness
about:
In this class, Hajime Kinoko teaches his Hip Harness for suspension with his model Maya Homerton.

Function meets form in this intermediate level harness. Kinoko’s hip harness is designed in such a way that it enables comfortable suspensions for every body types without demanding a high level of flexibility.

It offers sturdy hip support and reduces waist load (as opposed to Gorgone’s hip-harness designed for models with more back flexibility and who enjoy waist load), making it ideal if you’re looking to take some pressure off the lower back in bridge positions. This versatile tie is ideal for inversions and bridges and is solid enough to sustain dynamic transitions and self-suspensions.

Further information regarding the suspension line:

Kinoko's suspension line method for this tie is very simplified to allow the rigger to attach it easily and quickly during transition work (e.g. while the model is in a face-down and needs support quickly) and prioritizes efficiency over symmetry and balance. If you prefer, you can also use a normal Epsilon instead of the anchoring demonstrated in this tutorial.

The Moon Tie can be used by itself or together with any chest harness of your choice. It goes particularly well with the Neck-Hug tie for a refreshing combo or a Strappado, if you are looking for more of a challenge.

This minimalistic tie is inspired by a structure demonstrated by Boris Mosafir during one of his classes and revisited by Gorgone according to her own style. title: Tenshi Suspension
about:
In this shibari class, Ropunawa teaches the chest-free Tenshi Harness Suspension with his model Freya. The Tenshi was originally developed by Tifereth and is taught here with her permission.


In the follow-up to his class on the unconventional Tenshi Harness, Ropunawa delves further into the utility of this ingenious tie by demonstrating a full suspension with the tenshis. By lifting the Tenshi Harness to standing and then incorporating a Basket Tie to support the lower body, the chest-free harness can be used to create an eye-catching side suspension. From here, Ropunawa further explains various tricks to play with different heights, as well as showing how the tenshis can be brought to the front for an even more drastic change and evidence of the tie’s surprising versatility.


As with every tie though, the Tenshi Harness Suspension is not without its own important technique and safety considerations. Both riggers and models alike should be well-practiced in suspensions before attempting this class.

title: Simple Arm Harnesses
about:
In this step-by-step shibari course, Gorgone teaches examples of simple and fun arm ties with their model Jewelryandfire. These easy to execute arm harnesses use knots and frictions learned in the Beginner Course combined together to create a variety of full ties that can be tied on a partner.

The Arm Ladder Ties uses beginner knots and frictions to create an eye-catching and effective arms-in-front harness that can be a great introduction to body handling and floor play while also being comfortable and sustainable for the person being tied.

The Simple Neck Hug is an ideal tie to begin to play with a sense restriction in ropes, by wrapping the arms of the person being tied around their neck. However, it’s designed for safety too with a clever Yuki fix system incorporated to make untying quick and fuss-free.

Always remember to communicate with your partner to make sure the tie suits their specific needs and preferences. Make adjustments accordingly or untie and seek further advice from a skilled rigger if you cannot find an appropriate solution on your own.

title: Mini Leg Ties
about:
In this step-by-step shibari course, Fred Hatt teaches three simple leg ties – using only single- and double-column ties and minimal rope – with his model Briki.

In the Leg Hug class, it’s all about clever body positioning to create an effective and exposing tie using just one rope and one knot.

The Agura class teaches a straightforward variation of the classic Agura tie, which secures the legs to the waist in a cross-legged position using just a single-column tie and basic frictions.

The Creative Agura class offers a more strenuous take on the agura position by bringing the head down and forward towards the legs. Quick and easy to tie, it’s also quick and easy to release, making it ideal for beginners starting to play with more challenging positions.

These classes are suitable for all levels. Always feel free to adapt these leg ties to your partner's flexibility or preference and to experiment with different variations of these ties/concepts according to your own imagination.

For those who don’t already know how to tie the basic knots used in these classes, you can learn the Single-Column Tie or Double-Column Tie in our Beginner Course. For those who do, any single-column tie of your choice can be used in this class.

title: Ichinawa | One Rope Play (FREE)
about:
Tying with one rope only is often called Ichinawa, from the Japanese "ichi" (one) and "nawa" (rope). In this video, Gorgone demonstrates in a short session with her model Jewerlyandfire what can be done with a single rope by using and combining the concepts and techniques that she teaches in the Shibari Beginner Course.

Shibari can be highly technical and intricate but before loosing ourselves in the fancy techniques, we should remember that bondage can also be a sensual, playful and emotional practice. The rope is an extension of our body. We can use it to restrain, move, pull, push, squeeze... It can be soft and gentle like a caress or rough and assertive. The panel of sensations and emotions available is infinite!

Rope is only a tool to communicate; it’s the language, not the subject. The key elements of a rope dialogue are rhythm (fast/slow), space (close/far) and tightness (strong/soft). Pauses and variations of those elements are important to keep the dialogue dynamic and interesting.

The Basket Tie is a popular and classic shape that has taken Shibari Study students all the way from basic beginner ties to supportive suspensions and simple-yet-challenging inversions. As taught by Ropunawa, the Half Basket offers a twist on the familiar full version, only capturing one leg to the waist. Because the Half Basket is less stable than its full counterpart, it’s important to understand the risks involved, which Ropunawa details in this class. As always, please only attempt suspending from this tie if you have prior experience with suspensions.

title: Rolling The Dice
about:
In this shibari tutorial, Lief and Icky share Rolling the Dice, another fun labbing-for-better-rope game, this time using dice to help you practice better body manipulation and get more creative in rope.

It’s time to take overthinking out of your rope and leave it to a roll of the dice. While memorizing various patterns and harnesses has its place in shibari, this playful game challenges riggers and bottoms to be creative, reimagine how various parts of the body can be connected, and get flexible (sometimes even literally). As Lief and Icky explain, each side of the dice correlates with a different body part – which parts is up to you and how you tie them together after rolling your dice is definitely up to you. Remember that you’re allowed to veto the dice too: if something doesn’t feel doable for whatever reason, you can always roll again.

This exercise is suitable for all levels, as long as you allow your own skill set to guide you. Thinking outside the box in your rope practice is a valuable skill at every level.

title: Geeking About The Single-Column Tie
about:
In this shibari course, Fuoco takes a deep dive into one of the most widely used and important fundamental ties in shibari with her model Cat: the single-column tie (SCT).

Whether you’re still fairly new to shibari or you’ve been tying for a while, the single-column tie is likely one of the first ties you learnt and an invaluable building block in your rope practice. This four-part course is all about understanding how that building block works in order to use it as effectively as possible and ultimately make your single-column ties more robust and reinforced. With an in-depth exploration of various types of single-column tie, considerations for smarter tying with each, plus a game to test all your new single-column tie know-how, it’s time to get geeking…

The first class explores collapsible ties and parallel directionality. Square knot, granny knot, reef knot… Whatever you call them, this one is all about collapsible single-column ties and how your running line moves out of your cuff at a parallel.

Now that you’ve got the hang of parallel directionality, let’s add a twist. The second class is all about collapsible ties and perpendicular directionality and how to build sturdier ties when your running line takes a turn out of your cuff.

In the third class, Fuoco explores non-collapsible ties and perpendicular directionality, explaining why tying with directionality in mind still matters when you’re using Somerville bowlines or other forms of non-collapsible single-column tie.

Finally, in the last part of the course, it’s time for a game of Single-Column Tie Twister to test your skills.

This course is suitable for all levels, though some confidence with rope handling and experience tying single-column ties is beneficial.

title: Xana Partial Suspension
about:
In this class Gorgone and her model Xana demonstrate a simple partial suspension using the Xana Harness and Diamond Leg Tie.

Playing around with low suspensions and only part of the body lifted off the floor is a safer and less stressful way to practice suspensions for riggers and/or models with less experience or confidence. It is also a wonderful way to explore suspension sensations in a more relaxed, playful or intimate way, rather than focusing on complicated, stressful and challenging techniques.

If you are new to suspensions, we recommend that you watch our Uplines & Lock-offs 101 course!

Related videos:

  • Xana Harness

  • Xana Self-Suspension

title: Minimalism Performance (FREE)
about:
In this mesmerizing inspiration session from Docvale and Bänana, the French rope educators and life partners demonstrate their take on minimalism in rope bondage, exploring how even a “classic” suspension using a minimal amount of rope can be an impactful tool to communicate different intentions and emotions.


After four years of practicing ropes together, Docvale and Bänana have frequently repeated this minimalistic sequence together. However, as they explain in the feedback video following the session, the emotions that come up are always different and sometimes using fewer ropes can actually be a catalyst for a more dynamic tying experience.

title: Self-Suspension Safety Talk
about:
In this shibari class, KissmedeadlyDoll sits down for some self-suspension safety real talk aimed at solo rope practitioners.

Easy there, self-tyer! Before you get yourself into a bind that you can’t get out of, put your ropes aside and get real with KissmedeadlyDoll as she dives deep into safety for self-suspension. As a self-tyer and self-suspender with more than a decade’s experience, Doll has learned a few tricks along the way… and fucked up a couple of times too. In this shibari safety lecture, she shares everything she knows – and everything she wishes she’d known – to help make your first forays into self-suspending safer, smoother and more confident. From planning and managing risk to emergency back-up plans, this is essential viewing for everyone who’s their own rigger and model all rolled up into one.

This class is suitable for all levels, though the techniques discussed in this class are aimed at self-tying practitioners who are already starting to explore suspensions. As KissmedeadlyDoll explains, being cognizant of “when are you ready to self-suspend?” is part of safer self-suspension, so please be mindful of your own skill set as you decide if you’re ready to elevate your bondage practice.
